global temperature.name: Global Temperature
global temperature.description: Rising long-term temperature changes the baseline that weather now operates on, making heat extremes, heavy rainfall, and stress on ice, crops, and ecosystems more likely.
incoming: Carbon dioxide traps heat that would otherwise escape to space. As emissions accumulate in the atmosphere, global temperatures rise.

Methane traps heat very effectively, so releasing more of it raises global temperatures, especially over the next few decades. Cutting methane emissions can therefore slow near-term warming faster than reductions in longer-lived gases alone.

Reduced marine low-cloud cover reflects less sunlight and amplifies warming. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assesses the subtropical marine low-cloud feedback as positive with high confidence.

Declining reflective aerosol forcing removes part of the historical masking of greenhouse-gas warming. Human-caused aerosols exert a net negative heat-trapping influence, so reducing that negative forcing can add near-term warming unless greenhouse-gas forcing falls sufficiently at the same time.
Land carbon sink weakening amplifies temp by leaving more emitted carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of land carbon sink weakening.

Ocean carbon uptake weakening amplifies temp by increasing the airborne fraction of carbon emissions. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of ocean carbon uptake weakening.

Removing forest changes water loss from soil and plants, latent and sensible heat, roughness, turbulent mixing, absorbed solar radiation and heat storage locally, while atmospheric and oceanic adjustments create nonlocal responses. Forest-carbon loss adds a separate greenhouse-gas warming process.

Nitrous oxide absorbs heat in the atmosphere and remains there for a long time, adding to global warming alongside carbon dioxide and methane. Its long atmospheric lifetime and strong infrared absorption add a warming influence, contributing to warming alongside other greenhouse gases.
Coal power releases carbon dioxide within its reported sector and geography. As the gas builds up in the atmosphere, it raises global temperatures.
Gas power releases carbon dioxide within its reported sector and geography. As the gas builds up in the atmosphere, it raises global temperatures.
Oil fired power releases carbon dioxide within its reported sector and geography. As the gas builds up in the atmosphere, it raises global temperatures.
Coal industrial heat releases carbon dioxide within its reported sector and geography. As the gas builds up in the atmosphere, it raises global temperatures.
outgoing: Warmer air can contain more water vapour, increasing moisture convergence and event-scale precipitation intensity when lifting and storm dynamics are present. Additional warming increases the moisture ceiling available to the heaviest precipitation events.

Warming can increase ecosystem respiration, drought and fire losses and thaw frozen carbon, raising natural net carbon release or weakening uptake. This is a carbon-climate feedback, not the original human-caused emissions driver.

Warming can enhance microbial methane production in waterlogged wetlands and can expose thawed permafrost carbon. The net atmospheric response depends on hydrology, oxidation, transport and concurrent human-caused emissions.
A warmer atmosphere and ocean hold more heat and moisture. This makes extreme heat, heavy rain, drought, and several hazards happening together more likely.

A warmer baseline raises both heat and atmospheric moisture capacity, making dangerous heat-humidity combinations more likely and pushing wet-bulb exposure closer to physiological limits. Within tropical land regions between 20 degrees South and 20 degrees North, climate models constrained by atmospheric dynamics project regional extreme wet-bulb temperature to rise with tropical-mean warming.

Rising temperatures alter land-ocean thermal contrast and moisture loading, which can destabilize monsoon timing and rainfall intensity even though regional circulation details still matter. Warming and greenhouse-gas forcing can intensify persistent hot-night exposure and alter drought or monsoon characteristics, but the sign, magnitude and event definition remain region-, season- and mechanism-specific.

Rising surface temperatures increase active-layer depth and thaw frozen ground, making permafrost thaw one of the clearest direct frozen-water system responses to planetary warming. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of warming.

Warming shifts winter precipitation from snow toward rain and increases midwinter melt, raising the chance of rain-on-snow runoff and flood damage in cold regions. Warming can increase rain-on-snow flood risk in snow-covered basins by raising freezing levels, shifting winter precipitation toward rain, and accelerating melt when rain, snow-water equivalent, soil saturation, and basin routing align.

Warming initially raises glacier meltwater production but continued ice loss reduces glacier area, so many glacier-fed basins ultimately pass a runoff maximum and enter declining long-term meltwater contribution. Warming alters glacier and sea-ice energy balance, ocean heat and freshwater structure, and carbon uptake.

Warming shifts precipitation phase and accelerates snow loss, making higher temperature an upstream driver of snow-drought risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of warming.

Higher temperatures can reduce takeoff performance and amplify runway and operations stress, making warming an upstream pressure on airport climate exposure. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of warming.

Urban tree canopy can decline under rising heat, drought stress, and compounding urban pressures, especially where maintenance and water access lag. Global Temperature raises pressure on through heat and drought stress.

human.summary: Global warming raises heat exposure, reduces safe outdoor work hours, increases drought and flood losses, and makes more neighborhoods costly to cool or protect.
consequences: Heat illness, kidney stress, and excess mortality rise during longer hot seasons.
Crop yields and livestock productivity fall as heat stress compounds drought.

planet.summary: Global temperature rise destabilizes multiple Earth systems at once by accelerating ice loss, ocean heat stress, biodiversity decline, and hydrologic disruption.
consequences: Heat stress pushes species beyond historical thermal niches and compresses viable habitat.
Snow, glacier, and sea-ice loss alter reflectivity and freshwater timing across regions.

response.defaultDriver: Continued net greenhouse-gas emissions from fossil energy, land-use change, infrastructure lock-in, and delayed investment keep adding warming and future adaptation costs.
levers: Cutting greenhouse-gas emissions rapidly across energy, land, transport, buildings, and industry.
Reaching net-zero carbon dioxide while reducing non-CO2 forcing to stabilize warming.

measurement.metric: Global mean surface temperature anomaly above 1850-1900
measurement.geography: global with land-ocean coverage diagnostics
measurement.cadence: monthly with annual synthesis

occurrences.title: Earth’s oceans just hit their hottest temperature ever—it’s only going to get worse

methane emissions.name: Methane Emissions
methane emissions.description: Methane is a powerful heat-trapping gas, so leaks from fossil systems and emissions from agriculture can speed up near-term warming.
incoming: Warming can enhance microbial methane production in waterlogged wetlands and can expose thawed permafrost carbon. The net atmospheric response depends on hydrology, oxidation, transport and concurrent human-caused emissions.

When thawed permafrost becomes waterlogged and oxygen-poor, microbes convert stored carbon into methane that can escape into the atmosphere. Permafrost thaw is a well-established methane-release feedback.

Food waste disposed in landfills decomposes anaerobically and produces methane, making this a direct waste-management emissions process. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of food waste.
Flooded rice fields create oxygen-poor soil where microbes produce methane. The gas then escapes through rice plants, bubbles, and the water surface.
Through thawed, waterlogged carbon decomposition, Thermokarst Expansion can increase Methane Emissions. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of thermokarst expansion increases.

Methane Leak Detection and Repair reduces Methane Emissions when observations trigger verified repair. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Methane produced in thawing tundra soils, wetlands and lakes can escape into the atmosphere when microbial production exceeds oxidation. The added methane strengthens near-term warming, although flows vary sharply with soil moisture, temperature and transport processes.
Livestock, manure, rice, and other intensive agricultural practices can release methane. The magnitude depends on production system and management.

Expansion of unfrozen, permeable processes beneath thawing terrain or lakes can enable methane production and release where organic carbon and low-oxygen conditions are present. Use only within the geography, system boundary, and exposure conditions stated by the cited evidence.

Anaerobic decomposition of liquid manure produces methane unless gas is captured and destroyed or used. Apply only within the named basin, airshed, production system, or humanitarian response context.

More ruminants generally increase total enteric methane within the herd boundary, while diet and productivity alter emissions per animal and per unit product. Apply only within the named basin, airshed, production system, or humanitarian response context.
outgoing: Methane traps heat very effectively, so releasing more of it raises global temperatures, especially over the next few decades. Cutting methane emissions can therefore slow near-term warming faster than reductions in longer-lived gases alone.

Methane traps substantially more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide over the near term, adding warming that can intensify heat, rainfall and other climate extremes. Co-occurring or sequential heat, heavy-rainfall, drought, wildfire, cyclone, and flood hazards.

Methane adds to the near-term warming burden that raises humid heat exposure. Combined heat and humidity extremes push human survivability limits, reduce labor capacity, and strain power, health, and cooling systems during prolonged heat events.

Methane emissions add strong near-term warming, changing atmospheric moisture and circulation in ways that can alter monsoon timing and rainfall variability. Erratic monsoon onset, breaks, and retreat intensify flood-drought swings, destabilizing food production, water storage, and hydro-dependent economies.
More methane uses up chemicals in the air that normally help remove it. With less of this natural cleaning capacity available, methane can remain in the atmosphere longer.
Higher globally averaged abundance increases direct forcing and also affects ozone and stratospheric water vapour. Overlap with other absorbers is included in the assessment method.

human.summary: Methane speeds up near-term warming, making heat, crop losses, and ozone-related respiratory harm arrive sooner.
consequences: Extra warming amplifies dangerous heat seasons within policy and infrastructure timescales.
Methane-driven ozone damages crops and increases breathing conditions in polluted regions.

planet.summary: Methane speeds up near-term planetary heating and increases ozone damage, feedback risk, and ecosystem stress on timescales short enough to outrun slow adaptation.
consequences: Fast warming raises the chance of crossing ecological thresholds before recovery buffers can respond.
Ozone damages plant tissue and suppresses photosynthesis in crops and wild vegetation.

response.defaultDriver: Atmospheric methane remains a high-leverage warming gas.
levers: Prevent Methane Emissions at its source through enforceable emissions, discharge, product, or process standards.
Measure Anthropogenic methane emissions by source sector at the facilities and places where exposure or ecological damage can occur.

measurement.metric: Anthropogenic methane emissions by source sector
measurement.geography: global, country, basin, facility class, or inventory jurisdiction
measurement.cadence: annual with source-specific updates

occurrences.title: Methane emissions are turbocharging climate change. These quick fixes could slow it down

deforestation.name: Deforestation
deforestation.description: Forest loss removes carbon storage, dries out landscapes, weakens rainfall cycles, and leaves soils and species more exposed.
incoming: Verified clearing of prior forest for subsequent oil-palm establishment is a direct agricultural land-use conversion and therefore a defined component of deforestation. Tree-cover loss or later oil-palm presence alone is insufficient.

High-volume, short-use fashion demand can increase procurement of new leather and bio-based fibres. Where bovine leather originates from cattle expansion in a forest-risk frontier, or forest-derived cellulosic fibre lacks deforestation-free traceability, clothing and footwear demand can transmit commodity pressure into forest conversion.

Demand for cattle, feed, oil crops and other agricultural commodities can increase production incentives and land requirements. Where yield growth, intensification, trade, governance or use of existing cleared land do not absorb that demand, producers can expand pasture or cropland by converting forest to agricultural land.

Horizontal expansion of settlements, roads and urban infrastructure can replace forest with built land, producing permanent land-use conversion. Outward expansion of settlements and infrastructure can permanently convert forest to built land and therefore cause a bounded share of deforestation.
Forests are permanently converted to cropland or pasture to expand agricultural production. Agricultural expansion for cropland and livestock is the dominant direct global driver of deforestation.

Mine footprints and associated infrastructure remove forest cover and open previously inaccessible forest to additional land conversion. Mining can directly clear forest at extraction sites and indirectly expand forest loss through access roads, settlements, and induced activity.
outgoing: Forest clearing fragments habitat when it divides previously contiguous forest into smaller or more isolated patches and increases edge exposure. Research supports this direct process: deforestation creates forest_fragmentation when clearing divides contiguous habitat.
Deforestation directly weakens land carbon sink weakening by removing biomass and degrading soils. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of deforestation.

Forest clearing and fragmentation remove food, shelter and stable microclimates for insects, reducing biomass where remaining habitat cannot support viable populations. Deforestation removes forage, nesting space, and microclimate stability, making it an upstream driver of insect biomass decline.

Removing forest cover exposes soil to erosion, heat and faster organic-matter breakdown, gradually reducing the humus that supports fertility and water retention. Deforestation strips litter inputs, canopy protection, and root structure from soils, accelerating the loss of humus and other organic matter.

Fragmentation and forest degradation can reduce resilience to heat, drought, pests, and fire, contributing to dieback where these stressors coincide. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Forest clearing and fragmentation reduce water loss from soil and plants and moisture recycling, expand edges, and increase fire incidence. These effects can combine with climate change to favour a persistent lower-biomass state.

Removing forest changes water loss from soil and plants, latent and sensible heat, roughness, turbulent mixing, absorbed solar radiation and heat storage locally, while atmospheric and oceanic adjustments create nonlocal responses. Forest-carbon loss adds a separate greenhouse-gas warming process.

Large-scale forest removal changes surface reflectivity, surface roughness, water loss from soil and plants and moisture recycling. The resulting land-temperature and hemispheric-energy contrasts can alter pressure gradients, cross-equatorial flow, monsoon circulation and rainfall.

Forest conversion changes canopy, light, temperature, standing water, predators, host communities and human contact patterns. In some tropical settings these changes favor mosquito species that transmit human pathogens, increasing vector abundance or richness and creating conditions that can support disease emergence or geographic expansion.

Clearing forest within a watershed removes canopy and root structure, reducing forest cover while increasing erosion and rapid runoff into streams. Deforestation can condition watershed forest loss through the reviewed biodiversity mechanism.

Clearing peatland vegetation commonly accompanies drainage and land conversion, disrupting hydrology, exposing peat, and removing the plant community that sustains peat formation. Promoted from exact-term ontology research only within the documented mechanism and scope.
Forest removal changes interception, rooting, soil structure, water loss from soil and plants, and runoff. In documented settings faster surface runoff reduces water reaching recharge zones.

human.summary: Forest loss removes rainfall buffering, destabilizes water supplies, and undermines food, income, and safety for communities that depend on intact landscapes.
consequences: Dry-season fires and smoke raise respiratory illness and destroy homes and assets.
Rainfall becomes less reliable as forest moisture recycling weakens.

planet.summary: Deforestation fragments habitat, weakens carbon sinks, alters rainfall recycling, and reduces whole-biome resilience.
consequences: Species lose connected habitat and face rising extinction risk as landscapes are fragmented.
Forest-rainfall feedbacks weaken, making dry seasons longer and ecosystems more fire-prone.

response.defaultDriver: Agricultural expansion is the dominant global direct driver, interacting with commodity demand, infrastructure, mining, weak land governance, insecure tenure, and enforcement gaps.
levers: Decoupling agricultural commodity production from forest conversion through traceable supply chains and enforceable land-use rules.
Securing Indigenous and community land rights and strengthening monitoring and enforcement where conversion pressure is high.

measurement.metric: Forest conversion and annual forest-area change
measurement.geography: bounded region first; aggregate only with reviewed spatial weights
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to source release

occurrences.title: Singapore spending billions to adapt to climate change, but deforestation continues

industry farming.name: Industry Farming
industry farming.description: Industrial farming drives up fertilizer use, water demand, and land stress, which can increase emissions, pollute waterways, and weaken soil health.
incoming: Demand growth is met partly through yield, stocking, and production-intensity increases when land expansion, imports, or demand reduction do not absorb it. Growth in demand for food, feed, fibre, and animal-source products increases pressure for higher-output and more intensive agricultural production systems.

Commercial livestock systems concentrate production by relying on larger and more standardized flows of maize, soy, protein meal, and other feed crops. Expansion of compound-feed-dependent livestock production is a major process of agricultural intensification.

External nutrient inputs raise attainable yields and support repeated high-output cropping where soil nutrients would otherwise constrain production. Availability and use of synthetic fertilizer is an enabling input for input-intensive crop-yield intensification.
outgoing: Irrigated agriculture is a major basin-scale withdrawal pressure, so intensive farming is an upstream contributor to baseline water stress. Persistent imbalance between water demand and available supply raises the baseline fragility of cities, farms, power systems, and river ecosystems.

Groundwater depletion is a direct process where irrigation and farm withdrawals outpace recharge over years to decades. Aquifers are being drawn down faster than they recharge, turning hidden water reserves into a long-lived constraint on farming, drinking water, and ecosystem resilience.

Industrial farming increases nutrient runoff risk because concentrated fertilizer use often outruns field uptake and enters waterways. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of industry farming.
Industry farming can embed irrigation water inefficiency through poorly matched application and conveyance losses. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of industry farming.
Industry farming can accelerate soil humus decline through intensive disturbance and low organic-matter return. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of industry farming increases.
Industry farming can accelerate topsoil erosion acceleration through intensive tillage and exposed soil. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of industry farming.

Industry farming can contribute to insect biomass decline through habitat simplification and intensive chemical exposure. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of industry farming.

Dependence on synthetic fertilizer exposes industrial farming to natural-gas prices, trade restrictions and supply disruptions that can rapidly raise input costs. Input-intensive industrial farming is directly exposed to fertilizer price shocks because nutrient costs feed quickly into planting decisions and food-system margins.

Concentrated livestock production creates sustained demand for maize, soy and other feed crops, tying animal output to cropland, fertilizer, water and trade. Industrial livestock systems deepen dependence on feed-crop supply chains that transmit land, water, and fertilizer stress through animal production.

High stocking pressure and repeated trampling, especially on wet soils, can compact rangeland and pasture soils. Use only within the geography, system boundary, and exposure conditions stated by the cited evidence.
Persistent Pesticide Residues in Sediment and Biota

Historical or current agricultural use can load persistent compounds into watershed soils and sediments, which may expose aquatic organisms and consumers long after the original application. Most pesticide mass applied in agriculture is not necessarily persistent or bioavailable, and current land use cannot identify the source of a legacy compound without historical and chemical evidence.

Crop-protection chemicals applied to fields can dissolve in water, bind to eroded particles, move through tile drains, or leach and discharge to streams. The process depends strongly on the compound and management.

human.summary: Industrial farming concentrates food output, pollution, labor exposure, and animal disease risk into a single system that can fail expensively for both producers and consumers.
consequences: Nutrient runoff contaminates rivers and raises drinking-water treatment burdens.
Workers and livestock face heat stress that cuts productivity and raises mortality risk.

planet.summary: Industrial farming drives nutrient overload, soil degradation, biodiversity simplification, and freshwater ecosystem stress.
consequences: Nutrient runoff fuels algal blooms and oxygen depletion in downstream waters.
Monoculture landscapes reduce pollinator diversity and ecological redundancy.

response.defaultDriver: Input subsidies, procurement and commodity incentives, concentrated supply chains, dietary demand, and prices that omit environmental and health costs reward throughput over resilience.
levers: Reducing nitrous oxide from fertilizer, methane from livestock and rice, and carbon losses from soils with measured, place-specific management.
Reforming support and procurement so soil, water, health, and biodiversity outcomes affect production incentives.

measurement.metric: Agricultural input-intensity profile
measurement.geography: bounded region first; aggregate only with reviewed spatial weights
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to source release

occurrences.title: Drugs, hormones and excrement: the polluting pig mega-farms supplying pork to the world

agricultural demand.name: Agricultural Demand
agricultural demand.description: Diet compares familiar foods directly, so users can see how beef, dairy, poultry, grains, and plant proteins differ on the same food-footprint scale.
incoming: The Indian Ocean Dipole can bring drought to some farming regions and heavy rain to others. Harvest impacts depend on where crops are grown and how farms prepare.
Livestock disease pressure disrupts food through mortality, reduced productivity, and movement controls. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of livestock disease pressure.
Fertilizer price shock raises pressure on food through higher input costs and constrained production. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of fertilizer price shock increases.
Agricultural labor exposure reduces reliability of food through heat-related labor capacity loss. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of agricultural labor exposure.
Feed crop dependency transmits risk into food when feed shortages constrain livestock production. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of feed crop dependency.
Cold chain failure risk reduces usable supply of food through spoilage and unsafe storage. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of cold chain failure risk.

El Niño-related heat, drought and flooding can reduce harvests and interrupt food supplies in exposed production regions. This edge represents El Niño–Southern Oscillation-related crop and fishery disruption processes into food-system stress.

La Niña can bring destructive rainfall to some farming regions and drought to others, disrupting harvests, fisheries and the reliability of regional food supplies. This edge captures El Niño–Southern Oscillation-linked agricultural and fishery stress processes into food volatility.

Extreme heat and humidity reduce safe working hours for farm labor and can stress crops and livestock, lowering food production in exposed regions. This edge captures labor productivity loss and crop stress under combined heat-humidity extremes.

Unreliable monsoon timing and rainfall disrupt planting, irrigation and harvests, reducing agricultural output where food production depends heavily on the seasonal rains. Monsoon volatility is a direct process into food-production disruption.
outgoing: Food moving through production, storage, distribution, retail, and consumption creates stage-specific opportunities for loss and waste. It is not a fixed conversion of demand into waste.

Demand for cattle, feed, oil crops and other agricultural commodities can increase production incentives and land requirements. Where yield growth, intensification, trade, governance or use of existing cleared land do not absorb that demand, producers can expand pasture or cropland by converting forest to agricultural land.

Demand for agricultural commodities induces production and supply-chain activity. Fossil fuels and fossil-generated electricity used for machinery, fertilizer manufacture, processing, refrigeration, transport and retail emit carbon dioxide.

Demand for high crop yields drives production of nitrogen, phosphate and potash fertilizers used to replenish nutrients removed during harvest. Industrial fertilizer production ties fossil gas, ammonia synthesis, nitrous oxide risk, and runoff-intensive farming systems together.

Demand growth is met partly through yield, stocking, and production-intensity increases when land expansion, imports, or demand reduction do not absorb it. Growth in demand for food, feed, fibre, and animal-source products increases pressure for higher-output and more intensive agricultural production systems.

Sustained demand for rice can expand or intensify flooded cultivation, increasing the activity base when yields, trade, diets, and water availability do not offset the response. Crop, water regime, and management remain explicit.

Demand for edible oils and palm-containing food and consumer products can increase production and land demand. Forest clearance occurs only where added supply is met through plantation expansion into forest rather than yield gains, replanting, stocks, substitution, or expansion on already-cleared land.

human.summary: Agricultural demand hits people when food systems overuse land and water, making diets more expensive and supply chains more fragile.
consequences: Staple and protein prices rise when demand growth outruns climate-stressed supply.
Cropland and grazing expansion intensify land clearing and water withdrawals.

planet.summary: Global agricultural demand for food, particularly meat and dairy.
consequences: Demand for cattle, feed, oil crops and other agricultural commodities can increase production incentives and land requirements.
Demand for agricultural commodities induces production and supply-chain activity.

response.defaultDriver: Global supply chains prioritize low-cost animal proteins and processed grains, locking consumers into high-footprint defaults.
levers: Restructuring agricultural subsidies to disincentivize intensive livestock feed crops and reward low-footprint protein diversification.
Implementing land-protection mandates that block supply chain financing for commodities grown on deforested or conversion-exposed soils.

measurement.metric: Apparent domestic agricultural commodity demand
measurement.geography: country or declared market region
measurement.cadence: annual

occurrences.title: Boosting soybean protein: Zinc and sulfur essential in sustainable crop production

urbanization.name: Urbanization
urbanization.description: Urban expansion replaces vegetated land with heat-absorbing surfaces, raising heat exposure, runoff, and flood risk.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Urban growth can expand built area and housing footprints where development takes a low-density or outward-growth form. Legacy edge upgraded with relationship-specific authoritative evidence and bounded scope.

Population and economic growth can raise municipal demand faster than sources, networks, treatment, and loss control expand, increasing the likelihood of intermittent supply or scheduled restrictions during scarcity. Urban growth need not produce rationing when supply, reuse, efficiency, and infrastructure keep pace.

Urbanization simultaneously changes population density, household size, buildings, transport, public infrastructure, industrial structure, income, technology, land cover and energy intensity. These processes can raise or lower territorial carbon emissions, and spatial spillovers can transfer part of the response to adjacent regions.

Horizontal expansion of settlements, roads and urban infrastructure can replace forest with built land, producing permanent land-use conversion. Outward expansion of settlements and infrastructure can permanently convert forest to built land and therefore cause a bounded share of deforestation.

Urban population growth, construction, consumption and industrial concentration can raise blue-water demand and grey-water pollution pressure within and beyond administrative boundaries. Agglomeration, industrial restructuring, infrastructure and water-efficiency improvements can moderate or reverse the net effect at higher development levels.

Urban population, income and business activity can increase demand for air travel, provided fares, airport capacity and alternatives do not offset that growth. Urbanization can condition aviation demand growth through the reviewed infrastructure mechanism.

Urban growth concentrates food retail, restaurants and households, increasing potential waste volumes while logistics and collection systems determine how much is actually discarded. Loss and disposal across farms, retailers, kitchens, and landfills turn food systems into avoidable methane, water, and land-use pressure.

Urban growth adds cooled floor area and heat-retaining surfaces, increasing demand for air conditioning and its associated refrigerant stock. Cooling systems combine growing electricity demand with potent refrigerant leakage, making heat adaptation itself part of the climate story.

Dense populations, artificial containers, drainage gaps, mobility, and uneven vector control can increase vector-human contact and transmission persistence. Rapid or poorly serviced urbanization can expand habitat, host density, water-storage practices, and exposure networks favorable to some disease vectors.

Impervious urban drainage can route more rapid runoff into a combined sewer, raising overload pressure where capacity and storage are limited. Applies only where a combined sewer system and a documented overflow process exist.

Impervious surfaces, engineered drainage, and stream diversion can move precipitation rapidly to surface channels instead of allowing infiltration through recharge zones. Leaking utilities, recharge basins, and stormwater infiltration can locally maintain or increase recharge.

Development can remove habitat and introduce physical and behavioral barriers, collision risk, noise, light, and hostile land cover that reduce successful movement and gene flow between remaining patches. Some urban green spaces and backyards provide usable links, crossing structures can restore permeability, and urban presence alone does not establish a barrier for every species.

human.summary: Urban expansion can trap people in hotter, flood-prone places when housing, drainage, trees, and transit lag behind population growth.
consequences: Neighborhood heat and flood exposure rise when paving outpaces cooling and drainage.
Water, sanitation, and transport systems are strained by dense growth without resilience upgrades.

planet.summary: Urbanization can affect atmospheric chemistry and climate stability, biodiversity, habitat, and ecosystem resilience, and freshwater timing, quality, and aquatic habitat through Carbon Emission, Deforestation, and Baseline Water Stress.
consequences: Urbanization simultaneously changes population density, household size, buildings, transport, public infrastructure, industrial structure, income, technology, land cover and energy intensity.
Horizontal expansion of settlements, roads and urban infrastructure can replace forest with built land, producing permanent land-use conversion.

response.defaultDriver: The conversion of rural landscapes into dense urban settlements.
levers: Address the verified upstream pressures that increase Urbanization rather than treating the observed outcome in isolation.
Use Annual expansion of built-up surface to test whether policy or operational changes are reducing the condition.

measurement.metric: Annual expansion of built-up surface
measurement.geography: urban centre, metropolitan area, country, or declared grid
measurement.cadence: annual to multi-year remote-sensing update

fast fashion.name: Fast Fashion
fast fashion.description: High water use, petrochemical inputs, dye pollution, and waste give low-cost, short-lived clothing an impact that extends far beyond the store.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Fast fashion is linked to emissions through energy-intensive manufacturing and logistics. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of fast fashion.

Rapid clothing turnover increases demand for fibres, water, energy and chemical processing, accelerating resource use before garments reach the end of their practical life. This edge captures textile water demand and pollution pressure.

High-volume, short-use fashion demand can increase procurement of new leather and bio-based fibres. Where bovine leather originates from cattle expansion in a forest-risk frontier, or forest-derived cellulosic fibre lacks deforestation-free traceability, clothing and footwear demand can transmit commodity pressure into forest conversion.
High-volume textile production and short product lifetimes increase wastewater, dye, chemical, and waste burdens. The receiving-water effect depends on treatment and disposal controls.

human.summary: Fast fashion shifts water pollution, waste, and labor harm onto communities far from the checkout counter.
consequences: Untreated textile effluent contaminates local rivers used for drinking and irrigation.
Low-wage supply chains concentrate occupational exposure and wage vulnerability.

planet.summary: Fast Fashion can affect atmospheric chemistry and climate stability and biodiversity, habitat, and ecosystem resilience through Carbon Emission, Resource Depletion, and Deforestation.
consequences: Fast fashion is linked to emissions through energy-intensive manufacturing and logistics.
Rapid clothing turnover increases demand for fibres, water, energy and chemical processing, accelerating resource use before garments reach the end of their practical life.

response.defaultDriver: Fast fashion profit models rely on rapid turnover and low-cost petroleum-derived synthetic fabrics.
levers: Imposing extended producer responsibility (EPR) fees at the point of sale to finance textile recycling.
Enforcing strict microplastic filtration standards on industrial and household washing machines.

measurement.metric: Textile products placed on market and unsold textiles destroyed
measurement.geography: declared facility, industry class, country, trade region, or supply-chain boundary
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to production and inventory reporting

occurrences.title: AI machine sorts clothes faster than humans to boost textile recycling in China

migration.name: Migration
migration.description: Climate-linked displacement does not directly warm the planet, but it can push people into places where housing, water, health systems, and infrastructure are already under stress.
incoming: Repeated episodes of dangerous heat and humidity can make work and daily life unsafe, increasing pressure for temporary or permanent migration. Wet-bulb heat can make work and outdoor survival conditions untenable, increasing displacement pressure.

El Niño can damage harvests, water supplies and livelihoods through regional drought or flooding, increasing displacement pressure where households have limited capacity to recover. This edge is used for displacement pressure under El Niño–Southern Oscillation-linked drought, flood, and livelihood shocks.

Repeated monsoon failure or destructive rainfall can erode crops, income and housing, increasing migration when local recovery options are exhausted. Repeated monsoon failure or flood shocks raise displacement pressure.
Ground failure and infrastructure instability make permafrost thaw a direct habitability and relocation stressor. Undermines settlement stability for across Arctic communities.

Planned Relocation can reduce emergency displacement within Migration by moving before repeated disasters destroy housing and services. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.
Sustained food-access loss can contribute to livelihood displacement alongside conflict and economic factors. Apply only at the geography supported by the metric.

Carbon-dioxide emissions intensify climate hazards that damage homes, water supplies, harvests and livelihoods. Repeated losses can increase temporary displacement or longer-term migration when local recovery options are exhausted.

Loss of forest-derived livelihoods and ecosystem services can contribute to displacement pressures alongside economic, political, and climatic drivers. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
Climate hazards can contribute to displacement and migration alongside social, economic, and political drivers. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
outgoing: Displaced households enter recovery with unequal access to housing, insurance, savings, documentation and public aid, allowing migration shocks to widen existing recovery gaps. Displacement can widen recovery inequality when receiving regions and low-income households face very different capacity to absorb shocks and rebuild.

Large or repeated displacement can overwhelm the institutions responsible for housing, land, services and public participation during planned or emergency relocation. Migration pressure becomes an institutional issue when governments must plan housing, services, land access, and legal processes for relocation.

Large or rapid displacement can raise demand for shelter, food, health, water, and protection services in receiving and transit areas. Concurrent disasters, displacement, and conflict can raise the number of people requiring time-sensitive assistance faster than response capacity expands.

human.summary: Climate-linked migration becomes a crisis when housing, jobs, schools, and health systems in receiving regions cannot absorb displaced people safely.
consequences: Families lose stable housing, schooling continuity, and local support networks.
Receiving cities face pressure on clinics, water systems, and affordable housing.

planet.summary: Migration has no direct Earth-system outcome established in the current graph; its relevance is limited to the measured condition until a downstream ecological effect is verified.
consequences: No direct planetary consequence is inferred beyond the current evidence boundary for Migration.

response.defaultDriver: Displacement of populations driven by rising sea levels (monitored by Sentinel-6 and Jason altimetry) and severe drought indices derived from GRACE gravity mass changes.
levers: Change the finance, protection, and governance rules that allow Migration to concentrate losses on exposed households.
Fund early intervention using New internal displacement movements associated with recorded hazards rather than waiting for a crisis to become a permanent social or fiscal burden.

resource depletion.name: Resource Depletion
resource depletion.description: When extraction outpaces recovery, groundwater reserves fall, soils degrade, and the natural buffers communities rely on become weaker.
incoming: Mining and processing concentrate land, water, waste, and material depletion pressures. Primary mining, fossil-based plastics production and steelmaking increase demand for named raw materials and can raise economy-wide material footprint or domestic material consumption.

Battery supply pressure can deepen water and land depletion where extraction, refining, and waste burdens concentrate in mining regions. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of battery supply chain pressure.

Rapid clothing turnover increases demand for fibres, water, energy and chemical processing, accelerating resource use before garments reach the end of their practical life. This edge captures textile water demand and pollution pressure.

Carbon Dioxide Removal can increase Resource Depletion through land, water, energy, and material requirements. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Low-Carbon Cement and Concrete can reduce Resource Depletion when material-efficient design lowers virgin input demand. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Industrial heat that remains hard to decarbonize prolongs fuel, cooling, and materials demand across high-temperature manufacturing systems. Industrial Heat Decarbonization Gap raises pressure on through water and material demand.

Expanded extraction and declining ore quality can increase material throughput, energy use, waste, water pressure, and depletion of accessible high-grade resources. Primary mining, fossil-based plastics production and steelmaking increase demand for named raw materials and can raise economy-wide material footprint or domestic material consumption.
Virgin polymer production consumes fossil feedstocks, energy, water, and other materials. Circularity and recycled content can reduce the burden.
Conventional production requires large flows of ore, reductants, energy, and other materials. Efficiency, recycling, and lower-impact processes moderate demand.
outgoing: Resource depletion can intensify fertilizer price shock through energy and mineral input constraints. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of resource depletion.

Resource depletion can raise conflict risk escalation where scarcity interacts with weak institutions and inequality. Analyzes climate-induced disasters acting as conflict risk multipliers through displacement and food systems.

Sustained groundwater withdrawals that exceed natural or managed recharge turn wider resource pressure into measurable aquifer overdraft. Aquifer overdraft is a direct resource-depletion process where extraction continues past recharge for years or decades.

human.summary: Resource depletion hits people when aquifers, soils, and local reserves no longer support drinking water, farming, or stable household incomes.
consequences: Groundwater depletion raises pumping costs and can leave towns with unreliable water access.
Topsoil loss lowers farm productivity and increases dependence on costly inputs.

planet.summary: Resource depletion weakens land and water systems by exhausting the physical stocks they depend on.
consequences: Aquifer depletion reduces environmental flows and destabilizes freshwater ecosystems.
Soil exhaustion lowers biological productivity and makes landscapes less drought-resilient.

response.defaultDriver: Rapid depletion of fresh water aquifers and arable topsoil.
levers: Address the verified upstream pressures that increase Resource Depletion rather than treating the observed outcome in isolation.
Use Material footprint and domestic material consumption by raw-material class to test whether policy or operational changes are reducing the condition.

measurement.geography: UNSD country, region, or World geography with consumption-based and domestic-use boundaries separated

carbon emission.name: Carbon Emission
carbon emission.description: Carbon dioxide from fossil fuels and land-use change stays in the atmosphere for a long time, driving warming, ocean acidification, and long-lived climate pressure.
incoming: Warming can increase ecosystem respiration, drought and fire losses and thaw frozen carbon, raising natural net carbon release or weakening uptake. This is a carbon-climate feedback, not the original human-caused emissions driver.

Aviation demand growth is a direct upstream pressure on carbon emissions because most flights still rely on fossil jet fuel and high-altitude combustion. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of aviation demand growth.
Plastics and petrochemicals carry direct fossil-feedstock and process-energy emissions across production and end-of-life treatment. Adds through fossil feedstocks and process energy.

Continued operation of fossil peaker plants directly emits carbon dioxide during peak generation. Continued operation of fossil-fuel peakers, backup generators, diesel freight vehicles, coal-intensive steel capacity, and unabated industrial heat equipment sustains carbon-dioxide emissions.
Gas-fired power plants release carbon dioxide when they burn natural gas to generate electricity. Greater dependence on those plants increases cumulative emissions.

Continued reliance on fossil-fuel boilers and high-temperature process equipment sustains industrial carbon-dioxide emissions when cleaner heat technologies are unavailable or slow to replace them. Continued operation of fossil-fuel peakers, backup generators, diesel freight vehicles, coal-intensive steel capacity, and unabated industrial heat equipment sustains carbon-dioxide emissions.
Heating limestone into clinker releases carbon dioxide through the chemical reaction itself. Fuel burned to run the kiln adds another source of emissions.

Continued coal- and gas-intensive steel routes directly sustain carbon emissions. Continued operation of fossil-fuel peakers, backup generators, diesel freight vehicles, coal-intensive steel capacity, and unabated industrial heat equipment sustains carbon-dioxide emissions.

Fabrication electricity and fluorinated process gases contribute directly and indirectly to greenhouse-gas emissions. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of semiconductor fabrication footprint increases.

Diesel and gas backup generators emit carbon dioxide when operated. Continued operation of fossil-fuel peakers, backup generators, diesel freight vehicles, coal-intensive steel capacity, and unabated industrial heat equipment sustains carbon-dioxide emissions.
Curtailment can sustain fossil generation when clean output cannot reach demand. The effect depends on dispatch and storage.

Desalination dependence can add to carbon emission where desalination electricity remains fossil-intensive. The emissions depend on how much water is produced and whether the electricity comes from fossil or low-carbon sources.
outgoing: Carbon dioxide traps heat that would otherwise escape to space. As emissions accumulate in the atmosphere, global temperatures rise.
Human-caused carbon dioxide absorbed by seawater changes carbonate chemistry and lowers pH. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of carbon emission.
Through cumulative greenhouse warming, Carbon Emission drives pressure toward Ice Sheet Mass Loss. Compiles satellite observations of Greenland and Antarctic ice sheet mass loss.

Carbon-dioxide emissions warm the atmosphere, raising the baseline from which dangerous combinations of heat and humidity develop. Combined heat and humidity extremes push human survivability limits, reduce labor capacity, and strain power, health, and cooling systems during prolonged heat events.

Carbon-dioxide emissions raise heat trapped in the climate system and global temperature, altering atmospheric moisture and land-ocean temperature contrasts that help govern monsoon timing and rainfall intensity. Erratic monsoon onset, breaks, and retreat intensify flood-drought swings, destabilizing food production, water storage, and hydro-dependent economies.

Carbon emissions load the climate system with warming that contributes to sea-level rise, strengthening the baseline flood and erosion risk facing coasts. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of carbon emission increases.

Cumulative greenhouse emissions raise heat trapped in the climate system and warm the climate. Faster subpolar North Atlantic warming and enhanced high-latitude freshening increase buoyancy and layering that limits mixing, weakening deep-water formation and overturning.
Carbon-dioxide emissions warm the atmosphere, increasing the amount of water vapor it can hold. When storms have sufficient lift and moisture supply, that higher ceiling allows heavier precipitation.

Carbon-dioxide emissions add ocean and atmospheric heat that can provide more energy for tropical cyclones. In otherwise favorable conditions, warmer upper-ocean water increases the potential for rapid intensification.

Carbon Emission changes water loss from soil and plants and hydrologic conditions, increasing water-stress risk where demand and supply are already constrained. Cumulative carbon-dioxide emissions contribute to warming, and warming changes climate hazards that can propagate into drought, heavy precipitation, fire, water, crop, biodiversity and infrastructure outcomes.

Carbon-dioxide emissions raise baseline temperatures and make dangerous heat more frequent and intense. Longer exposure increases dehydration, cardiovascular strain and mortality, especially where cooling and health care are limited.

Carbon-dioxide emissions intensify heat and humidity, reducing the time people can safely perform strenuous outdoor or uncooled work. Workers face greater heat illness and productivity loss as safe work-rest limits are exceeded.

human.summary: Carbon emissions matter to people because they add long-lived warming that increases heat, flood, food, and infrastructure losses across decades.
consequences: Long-term warming locks in more intense heat, wildfire, flood, and sea-level damage.
Public budgets face escalating adaptation and disaster-recovery costs.

planet.summary: Carbon emissions are the core long-lived forcing that raises planetary heat and shifts multiple Earth systems toward persistent destabilization.
consequences: Persistent CO2 loading commits the planet to longer-lived warming and slower recovery.
Ocean heat and carbon uptake intensify marine stress and acidification pressure.

response.defaultDriver: Fossil infrastructure, production and consumption subsidies, and investment lock-in sustain emissions even where lower-emission technologies are available.
levers: Replacing unabated fossil energy with low-emission electricity and fuels while improving efficiency and reducing avoidable demand.
Ending investment patterns and subsidies that extend unabated fossil infrastructure beyond climate-compatible lifetimes.

measurement.geography: global, country, or reporting jurisdiction with inventory boundary declared
measurement.cadence: annual

personal conveyance.name: Personal Conveyance
personal conveyance.description: Heavy dependence on private vehicles raises oil demand and combustion emissions, adding both climate pollution and harmful local air pollution.
incoming: Public Transit Expansion reduces dependence on Personal Conveyance when service is frequent, affordable, and connected to destinations. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Walking and Cycling Networks reduce dependence on Personal Conveyance for short trips connected by safe routes. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.
outgoing: Road traffic is a transport source of outdoor air pollution exposure that contributes to respiratory and cardiovascular burden. Ambient ozone, particulates, and combustion by-products translate transport and industrial activity into chronic respiratory, cardiovascular, and mortality risk.
Road-oriented mobility requires extensive paved rights-of-way and parking. Conventional dark, impervious surfaces absorb solar energy, store heat, and release it to nearby air and runoff.

Gasoline- and diesel-powered private cars and vans oxidize fossil carbon during use and emit carbon dioxide through their exhaust. Electric vehicles move most use-phase emissions to electricity generation, while vehicle and infrastructure production remain separate lifecycle terms.

Where road-fuel systems use palm-derived biodiesel, fuel demand and renewable-energy incentives can add feedstock demand that contributes to indirect production-area expansion into high-carbon-stock land unless additional supply is demonstrably low risk of indirect land-use change or comes from existing land and yield gains. The process is absent where palm is not used in transport fuel, and indirect land-use effects vary with feedstock sourcing, policy design, yields, land protection, substitution, and certification.

human.summary: Private vehicle dependence harms people through air pollution, fuel costs, unsafe streets, and high transport costs.
consequences: Traffic pollution increases asthma, cardiovascular stress, and chronic exposure near roads.
Households become more vulnerable to fuel-price spikes when daily life requires driving.

planet.summary: Personal Conveyance can affect atmospheric chemistry and climate stability through Carbon Emission and Urban Heat Island.
consequences: Gasoline- and diesel-powered private cars and vans oxidize fossil carbon during use and emit carbon dioxide through their exhaust.

Road-oriented mobility requires extensive paved rights-of-way and parking; conventional dark, impervious surfaces absorb solar energy, store heat, and release it to nearby air and runoff. Downstream changes in Asphalt Surface Heat Storage can then affect atmospheric chemistry and climate stability through Urban Heat Island.

response.defaultDriver: Car-dependent land use, subsidized road capacity, limited public transit, and fossil-fuel vehicle fleets keep daily travel centered on private motor vehicles.
levers: Reduce the emissions, land use, fuel dependence, and disruption associated with Personal Conveyance through cleaner modes and better network planning.
Use Personal passenger travel activity by transport mode to identify where efficiency, maintenance, redundancy, or demand alternatives have the greatest effect.

compound climate hazards.name: Compound Climate Hazards
compound climate hazards.description: Climate anomalies matter because they shift familiar seasonal patterns out of range, making floods, droughts, marine heat, and wildfire behavior harder to manage with historical expectations alone.
incoming: A warmer atmosphere and ocean hold more heat and moisture. This makes extreme heat, heavy rain, drought, and several hazards happening together more likely.

El Niño shifts tropical ocean temperatures and atmospheric circulation, which can align heat, drought, heavy rainfall and fire hazards across affected regions. El Nino is a canonical long-distance climate connection driver of global weather and climate anomalies.

La Niña reorganizes tropical rainfall and circulation, producing a different regional mix of floods, droughts and temperature extremes. La Nina is a canonical redistributor of drought, flood, and storm-track anomalies.

The Pacific Decadal Oscillation shifts ocean temperatures and weather patterns across the North Pacific and nearby continents over many years. Pacific Decadal Oscillation is a monitored natural mode that organizes regional sea-surface temperature and climate anomalies.
Decades-long swings in North Atlantic temperatures occur alongside changes in regional weather. This link does not mean people control the timing of the natural cycle.

Atlantic Nino and Nina phases are observed tropical Atlantic variability modes with rainfall and circulation teleconnections. Co-occurring or sequential heat, heavy-rainfall, drought, wildfire, cyclone, and flood hazards.

The Indian Ocean Dipole shifts rain and temperature patterns across East Africa, South Asia, Australia, and other connected regions. Operationally defined climate modes organize recurrent, phase-dependent circulation, temperature and precipitation anomaly patterns.

The Madden-Julian Oscillation helps shape where rain falls and how winds move across the tropics over the following weeks. Those week-to-week shifts can raise or lower the chance of heavy rain and dry spells across affected regions.

The phase of the North Atlantic Oscillation shifts winter temperatures, rain, storms, and the jet stream across the North Atlantic region. North Atlantic Oscillation phases organize observed temperature, rainfall, storm-track, and jet-stream anomalies across the North Atlantic sector.

The phase of the Arctic Oscillation shifts winter air pressure, temperatures, and winds across much of the Northern Hemisphere. Arctic Oscillation phases organize cold-season pressure, temperature, and circulation anomalies across the Northern Hemisphere.

The Pacific-North American pattern is linked with recurring shifts in temperature and rain across North America. Pacific-North American pattern phase is associated with documented North American temperature and precipitation anomaly patterns.
The Southern Annular Mode describes shifts in air pressure and westerly winds around Antarctica. Its phase changes weather across the Southern Hemisphere.
outgoing: Concurrent soil-water deficit, high temperature and elevated atmospheric vapour-pressure deficit increase evaporative demand, reduce hydraulic safety margins and carbon assimilation, and can interact with antecedent wetting, prior stress and biotic agents to trigger canopy defoliation, dieback and tree death. Coincident soil and atmospheric drought plus heat increase hydraulic and carbon stress and can cross species- and stand-specific mortality thresholds.

Compound climate hazards can include heavy-precipitation episodes where atmospheric conditions produce extreme rainfall. A warmer atmosphere can dump more water in short bursts, increasing the intensity of rainfall events that overwhelm drainage, utilities, and river management systems.
Compound climate hazards can include persistent agricultural and ecological drought in drying regions. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Compound climate hazards can include dangerous heat-humidity conditions where temperature and moisture align. Combined heat and humidity extremes push human survivability limits, reduce labor capacity, and strain power, health, and cooling systems during prolonged heat events.

Compound climate hazards can include rapidly intensifying tropical cyclones only in storm-prone basins with suitable ocean and atmospheric conditions. Warmer ocean conditions and favorable atmospheric setups can increase the likelihood that tropical cyclones intensify quickly before landfall, compressing preparation time and raising surge risk.
Compound climate hazards can include heat, drought, and fire-weather sequences that alter wildfire regimes when ignitions and fuels are present. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
Repeated heavy precipitation and flooding hazards can increase floodplain exposure where people and assets occupy inundation-prone areas. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Heat and compound hazard exposure can increase mortality burden where vulnerability, exposure, and health-system capacity align. Extreme heat becomes a mortality burden when exposure, age, chronic illness, housing, and care-system access combine beyond safe recovery limits.
Flood and heat hazards can elevate water-borne disease risk under inadequate water, sanitation, and hygiene controls. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
Heat, drought, heavy rainfall, and compound hazards can increase crop-yield volatility, subject to crop and management context. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Compound hazards can disrupt food production, access, and livelihoods alongside conflict, inequality, and market conditions. Uncertain or constrained physical and economic access to sufficient, safe, nutritious food.
Climate hazards can contribute to displacement and migration alongside social, economic, and political drivers. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

human.summary: Extreme weather shows up as human loss through damaged homes, interrupted services, food shocks, and emergency displacement.
consequences: Homes, roads, and power systems fail during storms, fires, and flood events.
Acute disasters interrupt schooling, medical care, and local employment.

planet.summary: Extreme anomalies reshape ecosystems through repeated disturbance, forcing species turnover and degrading habitat structure.
consequences: Repeated disturbance can prevent ecosystems from returning to prior stable states.
Species composition shifts as heat, fire, and flood-tolerant organisms replace others.

response.defaultDriver: Co-occurring or sequential heat, heavy-rainfall, drought, wildfire, cyclone, and flood hazards.
levers: Address the verified upstream pressures that increase Compound Climate Hazards rather than treating the observed outcome in isolation.
Use Days with concurrent climate-hazard threshold exceedances to test whether policy or operational changes are reducing the condition.

measurement.metric: Days with concurrent climate-hazard threshold exceedances
measurement.geography: bounded grid, city, basin, region, or country
measurement.cadence: daily classification with monthly and annual rollups

el niño.name: El Niño
el niño.description: El Nino redistributes tropical Pacific heat and shifts atmospheric circulation, which can change storm tracks, suppress rainfall in some regions, and increase flood risk or heat risk in others.
incoming: Weaker easterlies reduce eastern-Pacific upwelling and zonal thermocline tilt, reinforcing central and eastern equatorial Pacific warming through coupled feedback. Weak or reversed equatorial Pacific easterly trade-wind anomalies permit warm surface water and convection to shift eastward during El Niño development.

Recharge of warm water volume deepens the equatorial thermocline and supplies warm subsurface water that can reach the central and eastern Pacific after wind triggering. A positive equatorial Pacific upper-ocean heat-content anomaly preconditions, but does not guarantee, El Niño onset.

The active Madden-Julian Oscillation envelope can produce westerly wind bursts that launch downwelling Kelvin waves and move warm water eastward. Some Madden-Julian Oscillation events contribute to El Niño onset by organizing equatorial Pacific westerly wind bursts.
outgoing: El Niño shifts tropical ocean temperatures and atmospheric circulation, which can align heat, drought, heavy rainfall and fire hazards across affected regions. El Nino is a canonical long-distance climate connection driver of global weather and climate anomalies.

El Niño warming in the tropical Pacific shifts monsoon circulation and rainfall timing, raising the likelihood of weak, delayed or uneven rainy seasons in affected basins. El Nino is linked to monsoon timing and rainfall disruptions across multiple regions, including South Asia.

El Niño-related heat, drought and flooding can reduce harvests and interrupt food supplies in exposed production regions. This edge represents El Niño–Southern Oscillation-related crop and fishery disruption processes into food-system stress.

El Niño can damage harvests, water supplies and livelihoods through regional drought or flooding, increasing displacement pressure where households have limited capacity to recover. This edge is used for displacement pressure under El Niño–Southern Oscillation-linked drought, flood, and livelihood shocks.

El Niño reorganizes tropical convection and atmospheric circulation, producing sustained rainfall deficits in some regions. Weather deficits can persist through soil-moisture, river-flow, reservoir and peatland memory after the atmospheric anomaly develops, extending agricultural, water-related and fire-weather drought conditions.

El Niño can leave a multi-year imprint on North Pacific temperature and circulation, contributing to Pacific Decadal Oscillation variability alongside internal ocean dynamics. El nino can condition pacific decadal oscillation through the reviewed climate dynamics mechanism.

El Niño alters tropical winds and the Walker circulation, changing the east-west Indian Ocean temperature gradient that defines the Indian Ocean Dipole. El nino can condition indian ocean dipole through the reviewed climate dynamics mechanism.

El Niño shifts tropical Pacific convection, launching atmospheric wave trains that favor characteristic phases of the Pacific-North American pressure pattern. El nino can condition pacific north american pattern through the reviewed climate dynamics mechanism.

El Niño shifts tropical Pacific convection and background winds, modulating the strength, location and propagation of Madden-Julian Oscillation events. El nino can condition madden julian oscillation through the reviewed climate dynamics mechanism.

The winds and ocean-heat changes left after an El Niño can create Pacific conditions that favor a later La Niña event. El Niño-related wind stress and poleward heat discharge can leave a shallow thermocline and negative warm-water-volume anomaly favorable for La Niña.

Some El Niño events combine elevated coastal temperature with strong swell activity, degrading canopy condition and physically removing plants. Impacts vary sharply by latitude and exposure, and comparable habitat can remain relatively unaffected during the same event.

Warm eastern and central equatorial water moves deep convection eastward and reduces the normal east-west pressure contrast, weakening or displacing the zonal overturning cell. Events differ in location and strength, and no single warm episode establishes a long-term circulation trend.

human.summary: El Nino redistributes rainfall and ocean heat in ways that quickly hit food prices, fisheries, drought risk, and disease exposure across multiple continents.
consequences: Harvests weaken in drought-hit regions while floods damage crops elsewhere.
Fisheries can be disrupted as marine temperatures and nutrient patterns shift.

planet.summary: El Nino reorganizes ocean-atmosphere coupling, disrupting marine productivity, rainfall regimes, and ecosystem timing across continents.
consequences: Weakened upwelling reduces nutrient delivery and marine productivity.
Coral bleaching risk rises as surface waters remain unusually warm.

response.defaultDriver: The warming phase of the ENSO pattern.
levers: Use forecasts and observations of Oceanic Niño Index warm-phase anomaly to prepare exposed regions before El Niño changes seasonal conditions.
Update water, food, health, and emergency plans for the specific regional hazards associated with El Niño.

measurement.metric: Oceanic Niño Index warm-phase anomaly
measurement.geography: Niño 3.4 region with coupled tropical-Pacific context
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to source release

occurrences.title: High winds during El Niño could be deadly for England’s stressed trees, say experts

la niña.name: La Niña
la niña.description: La Nina cools the tropical Pacific surface while reorganizing circulation patterns, often strengthening rainfall in some basins, deepening drought in others, and changing the odds of seasonal extremes worldwide.
incoming: Stronger easterlies push warm surface water westward, steepen the thermocline, and enhance cold-water upwelling in the eastern equatorial Pacific. The signed equatorial Pacific trade-wind anomaly supports La Niña when easterlies are stronger, not weaker, than normal.

Discharged equatorial heat and a shallower thermocline allow stronger upwelling of colder subsurface water in the central and eastern Pacific. A negative equatorial Pacific warm-water-volume anomaly strongly favors subsequent La Niña cooling.

The winds and ocean-heat changes left after an El Niño can create Pacific conditions that favor a later La Niña event. El Niño-related wind stress and poleward heat discharge can leave a shallow thermocline and negative warm-water-volume anomaly favorable for La Niña.
outgoing: La Niña reorganizes tropical rainfall and circulation, producing a different regional mix of floods, droughts and temperature extremes. La Nina is a canonical redistributor of drought, flood, and storm-track anomalies.

La Niña shifts tropical circulation and moisture transport, changing monsoon timing and concentrating unusually wet or dry conditions across affected basins. La Nina is linked to altered monsoon strength and rainfall distribution across several basins.

La Niña can bring destructive rainfall to some farming regions and drought to others, disrupting harvests, fisheries and the reliability of regional food supplies. This edge captures El Niño–Southern Oscillation-linked agricultural and fishery stress processes into food volatility.

La Niña can reinforce cool North Pacific temperature patterns that resemble part of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation, although the longer-lived mode also has internal drivers. La nina can condition pacific decadal oscillation through the reviewed climate dynamics mechanism.

Cooler central and eastern equatorial water and a larger east-west gradient reinforce surface easterlies, western warm-water piling, and the normal rising-west sinking-east overturning pattern. The atmospheric response varies among events, and recent multi-decadal strengthening cannot be assigned to the cool phase or human-caused forcing without formal attribution.

human.summary: La Nina sharpens drought-flood contrasts, making some regions much drier while others face repeated flood and storm losses in the same season.
consequences: Water availability becomes less predictable as rainfall patterns swing harder.
Flood damage rises in exposed basins while drought losses mount elsewhere.

planet.summary: La Nina intensifies drought-flood contrasts and reorganizes ocean and rainfall conditions that many ecosystems depend on seasonally.
consequences: Hydrologic extremes stress both flood-adapted and drought-sensitive ecosystems.
Seasonal productivity and breeding cycles are disrupted when rainfall timing shifts abruptly.

response.defaultDriver: The cooling phase of the ENSO pattern.
levers: Use forecasts and observations of Oceanic Niño Index cool-phase anomaly to prepare exposed regions before La Niña changes seasonal conditions.
Update water, food, health, and emergency plans for the specific regional hazards associated with La Niña.

measurement.metric: Oceanic Niño Index cool-phase anomaly
measurement.geography: Niño 3.4 region with coupled tropical-Pacific context
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to source release

amoc slowdown.name: AMOC Slowdown
amoc slowdown.description: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation helps move heat, salt, and nutrients through the ocean, so a slowdown can reshape rainfall belts, sea level patterns, and marine ecosystem conditions around the Atlantic basin.
incoming: Cumulative greenhouse emissions raise heat trapped in the climate system and warm the climate. Faster subpolar North Atlantic warming and enhanced high-latitude freshening increase buoyancy and layering that limits mixing, weakening deep-water formation and overturning.

Added ocean heat changes seawater density and buoyancy, which can weaken the deep-water formation that helps sustain the Atlantic overturning circulation. Weakening Atlantic overturning circulation can redistribute heat, alter European and tropical rainfall, and increase the risk of abrupt regional climate disruptions.

Fresh meltwater from Greenland lowers North Atlantic surface salinity and density, making deep-water formation less efficient and potentially weakening Atlantic overturning. Weakening Atlantic overturning circulation can redistribute heat, alter European and tropical rainfall, and increase the risk of abrupt regional climate disruptions.

A fresher, more strongly stratified North Atlantic surface layer suppresses vertical mixing and deep-water formation, weakening a central process that drives Atlantic overturning. Weakening Atlantic overturning circulation can redistribute heat, alter European and tropical rainfall, and increase the risk of abrupt regional climate disruptions.
outgoing: Changes in the Atlantic overturning circulation alter how heat and salt move through the Atlantic, contributing to wider shifts in ocean-current patterns. A weaker circulation can redistribute warming, rainfall, and regional sea-level change around the Atlantic.

Atlantic overturning circulation variability can alter regional dynamic sea level along parts of the North Atlantic coast, changing inundation risk without determining global coastal outcomes. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of atlantic overturning circulation slowdown increases.

The northward western-boundary current forms an upper limb of Atlantic overturning, so changes in the overturning component can affect heat and volume transport through a monitored section even though winds and gyre circulation also sustain substantial flow. The surface current is not synonymous with basin-scale overturning, a stable section can coexist with changes elsewhere, and the wind-driven component may remain strong even if overturning weakens.

human.summary: AMOC slowdown harms people because it can rearrange rainfall, marine productivity, and coastal climate risks over regions that support hundreds of millions of livelihoods.
consequences: Rainfall shifts can destabilize food and water systems across the North Atlantic region and tropics.
Marine food webs and fisheries may be disrupted as circulation patterns weaken.

planet.summary: AMOC slowdown threatens large-scale ocean and climate regulation by shifting heat transport, rainfall patterns, and marine ecosystem structure.
consequences: Marine ecosystems can reorganize as nutrient, temperature, and current patterns change.
Regional rainfall stability weakens as ocean circulation no longer distributes heat the same way.

response.defaultDriver: Continued greenhouse-gas emissions, ocean warming, and freshwater input increase the risk of further AMOC weakening while infrastructure and food systems remain planned around historical circulation patterns.
levers: Integrating non-linear tipping risk into sovereign debt and real estate pricing models.
Deploying adaptive agricultural irrigation systems in areas vulnerable to rainfall shifts.

measurement.metric: Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation transport at a declared latitude
measurement.geography: named station, transect, depth layer, ocean region, or quality-controlled analysis grid
measurement.cadence: daily to monthly with annual synthesis
