wet-bulb heat.name: Wet-Bulb Heat
wet-bulb heat.description: High humidity makes extreme heat especially dangerous by limiting the body’s ability to cool itself through sweat.
incoming: A warmer baseline raises both heat and atmospheric moisture capacity, making dangerous heat-humidity combinations more likely and pushing wet-bulb exposure closer to physiological limits. Within tropical land regions between 20 degrees South and 20 degrees North, climate models constrained by atmospheric dynamics project regional extreme wet-bulb temperature to rise with tropical-mean warming.

Higher humidity directly limits evaporative cooling, increasing wet-bulb heat stress at a given air temperature. At a given dry-bulb temperature and pressure, increasing atmospheric moisture raises wet-bulb temperature and reduces the evaporative-cooling gradient available to people.

Carbon-dioxide emissions warm the atmosphere, raising the baseline from which dangerous combinations of heat and humidity develop. Combined heat and humidity extremes push human survivability limits, reduce labor capacity, and strain power, health, and cooling systems during prolonged heat events.

Methane adds to the near-term warming burden that raises humid heat exposure. Combined heat and humidity extremes push human survivability limits, reduce labor capacity, and strain power, health, and cooling systems during prolonged heat events.

Compound climate hazards can include dangerous heat-humidity conditions where temperature and moisture align. Combined heat and humidity extremes push human survivability limits, reduce labor capacity, and strain power, health, and cooling systems during prolonged heat events.
outgoing: Repeated episodes of dangerous heat and humidity can make work and daily life unsafe, increasing pressure for temporary or permanent migration. Wet-bulb heat can make work and outdoor survival conditions untenable, increasing displacement pressure.

Dangerous humid heat drives cooling-demand spikes that can push already stressed grids toward reliability limits. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of wet-bulb heat.

Extreme heat exposure raises heat-related illness and excess mortality, especially when humidity limits evaporative cooling. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of wet-bulb heat.

Wet-bulb heat directly intensifies occupational heat exposure because high humidity limits evaporative cooling and lowers safe labor capacity. Rising heat and humidity reduce safe work capacity, increase injury risk, and push labor-intensive sectors into direct climate-health loss.

Extreme heat and humidity reduce safe working hours for farm labor and can stress crops and livestock, lowering food production in exposed regions. This edge captures labor productivity loss and crop stress under combined heat-humidity extremes.

Humid heat becomes agricultural labor exposure when field work can no longer be sustained safely through the hottest parts of the day. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of wet-bulb heat increases.

Wet-bulb temperature combines air temperature and atmospheric moisture and therefore bounds evaporative cooling potential. As wet-bulb heat rises, sweat evaporation becomes less effective, body heat storage and cardiovascular and renal strain increase, and acute illness or mortality risk can rise, with strong variation by age, activity, acclimatization, housing and cooling access.

Extreme heat and humidity stress livestock, weaken immune defenses and can improve conditions for some pathogens and vectors, increasing disease pressure in exposed herds. Wet bulb heat can condition livestock disease pressure through the reviewed food mechanism.

High heat combined with humidity reduces safe working time and impairs livestock cooling, intensifying heat stress across farms. Wet bulb heat can condition farm heat stress through the reviewed food mechanism.

Extreme heat and humidity reduce aircraft takeoff performance and safe outdoor working time, constraining airport schedules and ground operations. Wet bulb heat can condition airport operational disruption through the reviewed infrastructure mechanism.

Extreme heat and humidity reduce safe dockworker hours, strain refrigerated cargo systems and lower equipment reliability at exposed ports. Wet bulb heat can condition port heat vulnerability through the reviewed infrastructure mechanism.

More frequent dangerous heat and humidity increases cooling demand, expanding air-conditioner use and the potential for refrigerant leakage. Cooling systems combine growing electricity demand with potent refrigerant leakage, making heat adaptation itself part of the climate story.

monsoon volatility.name: Monsoon Volatility
monsoon volatility.description: Shifts in monsoon timing and intensity can disrupt planting, reservoirs, flood control, and livelihoods even when total seasonal rainfall appears normal.
incoming: Rising temperatures alter land-ocean thermal contrast and moisture loading, which can destabilize monsoon timing and rainfall intensity even though regional circulation details still matter. Warming and greenhouse-gas forcing can intensify persistent hot-night exposure and alter drought or monsoon characteristics, but the sign, magnitude and event definition remain region-, season- and mechanism-specific.
Tropical Atlantic sea-surface temperature phases can modulate regional monsoon rainfall. Strength and sign depend on season and basin.

Indian Ocean Dipole phases alter Indian Ocean convection and rainfall patterns that modulate monsoon behavior. Indian Ocean Dipole state, Madden-Julian Oscillation phase and Walker-circulation displacement can redistribute tropical convection and moisture convergence, thereby modulating rainfall within named monsoon regions.

Madden-Julian Oscillation convection modulates active and break phases of multiple monsoon systems. Indian Ocean Dipole state, Madden-Julian Oscillation phase and Walker-circulation displacement can redistribute tropical convection and moisture convergence, thereby modulating rainfall within named monsoon regions.
Air pollution particles can change winds and rainfall. As particle levels rise or fall, monsoon timing and strength can shift, although the result varies widely by region.

El Niño warming in the tropical Pacific shifts monsoon circulation and rainfall timing, raising the likelihood of weak, delayed or uneven rainy seasons in affected basins. El Nino is linked to monsoon timing and rainfall disruptions across multiple regions, including South Asia.

La Niña shifts tropical circulation and moisture transport, changing monsoon timing and concentrating unusually wet or dry conditions across affected basins. La Nina is linked to altered monsoon strength and rainfall distribution across several basins.

Carbon-dioxide emissions raise heat trapped in the climate system and global temperature, altering atmospheric moisture and land-ocean temperature contrasts that help govern monsoon timing and rainfall intensity. Erratic monsoon onset, breaks, and retreat intensify flood-drought swings, destabilizing food production, water storage, and hydro-dependent economies.

Methane emissions add strong near-term warming, changing atmospheric moisture and circulation in ways that can alter monsoon timing and rainfall variability. Erratic monsoon onset, breaks, and retreat intensify flood-drought swings, destabilizing food production, water storage, and hydro-dependent economies.

Large-scale forest removal changes surface reflectivity, surface roughness, water loss from soil and plants and moisture recycling. The resulting land-temperature and hemispheric-energy contrasts can alter pressure gradients, cross-equatorial flow, monsoon circulation and rainfall.

Changes in the strength or longitude of zonal overturning alter where moist air rises and dry air subsides, shifting tropical rainfall and influencing some monsoon regions through atmospheric teleconnections. The response is not spatially uniform, circulation indices are partly diagnostic of the same rainfall field, and local monsoon dynamics can override the long-distance climate connection.
outgoing: Unreliable monsoon timing and rainfall disrupt planting, irrigation and harvests, reducing agricultural output where food production depends heavily on the seasonal rains. Monsoon volatility is a direct process into food-production disruption.

Repeated monsoon failure or destructive rainfall can erode crops, income and housing, increasing migration when local recovery options are exhausted. Repeated monsoon failure or flood shocks raise displacement pressure.

Seasonal wind and moisture-transport departures alter convergence, active-break timing, and the location of intense monsoon rainfall. Large monsoon circulation and moisture-transport anomalies can concentrate rainfall into more extreme regional events.

human.summary: Monsoon volatility hits people through failed planting calendars, flood losses, reservoir instability, and food-price shocks across densely populated regions.
consequences: Planting and harvest windows become harder to time, increasing farm losses.

permafrost thaw.name: Permafrost Thaw
permafrost thaw.description: As formerly frozen ground warms, it can subside, damage infrastructure, and release stored carbon and methane into larger climate feedbacks.
incoming: Rising surface temperatures increase active-layer depth and thaw frozen ground, making permafrost thaw one of the clearest direct frozen-water system responses to planetary warming. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of warming.

Faster Arctic warming deepens the seasonally thawed active layer and raises ground temperatures, accelerating permafrost loss. Frozen northern soils are thawing, releasing greenhouse gases, destabilizing roads and settlements, and amplifying Arctic carbon feedback loops.

Severe tundra or boreal fire can remove insulating moss, vegetation and organic soil, lower surface surface reflectivity and deepen the active layer, accelerating thaw of underlying permafrost relative to comparable unburned terrain. Frozen northern soils are thawing, releasing greenhouse gases, destabilizing roads and settlements, and amplifying Arctic carbon feedback loops.
outgoing: Thaw of ice-rich coastal permafrost reduces bluff strength and exposes sediment and ground ice to thermal and mechanical erosion. Thaw weakens ice-rich Arctic coastal ground and increases susceptibility to erosion, while seasonal sea-ice loss exposes darker ocean that absorbs more solar energy and contributes to the positive surface reflectivity feedback and amplified Arctic warming.

When thawed permafrost becomes waterlogged and oxygen-poor, microbes convert stored carbon into methane that can escape into the atmosphere. Permafrost thaw is a well-established methane-release feedback.

Thermokarst expansion is a direct landscape expression of thawing ice-rich permafrost and collapsing ground structure. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of permafrost thaw.

Persistent thaw enlarges unfrozen talik layers within permafrost, changing groundwater flow and ground stability. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of permafrost thaw increases.

Thaw exposes long-frozen organic matter to microbial decomposition, releasing carbon dioxide and, in waterlogged ground, methane into the atmosphere. This edge captures thaw-driven carbon release beyond methane alone.
Ground failure and infrastructure instability make permafrost thaw a direct habitability and relocation stressor. Undermines settlement stability for across Arctic communities.

Warming increases active-layer thickness and can thaw excess ground ice. The resulting loss of ground volume, differential settlement, subsidence, drainage change and slope instability can reduce foundation bearing capacity, distort embankments and disrupt transport or utility assets built on susceptible permafrost.

Permafrost thaw exposes previously frozen organic carbon to microbial decomposition. Where thawed tundra remains saturated, oxygen-poor decomposition produces methane that can escape through soil, water or vegetation.

Loss of persistent ice in joints removes cementing support and exposes fractured rock to seasonal water and thermal cycling. How strongly this effect develops depends on ice content, joint orientation, and slope angle.

Ground thaw changes drainage, nutrients, and disturbance patterns that can facilitate shrub expansion in some tundra landscapes. Use only within the geography, system boundary, and exposure conditions stated by the cited evidence.

Thaw of mountain or polar permafrost can alter moisture, substrate stability and cold microclimates on exposed nunataks, reducing the suitable area or persistence of specialised cold-adapted biotic habitat even where total ice-free rock area expands. Named polar or alpine nunatak with ground temperature, active-layer depth, substrate stability, snow persistence and species occupancy measured together.

human.summary: Permafrost thaw becomes a problem when ground failure breaks homes, roads, pipelines, and water systems in Arctic settlements while adding more warming pressure.

incoming: Warming shifts winter precipitation from snow toward rain and increases midwinter melt, raising the chance of rain-on-snow runoff and flood damage in cold regions. Heavy warm rainfall onto an existing snowpack can combine rainfall runoff with rapid snowmelt, producing enhanced flood risk in snow-covered basins. outgoing: Rain falling onto an existing snowpack adds weight and liquid water while weakening bonds between snow layers. On steep pass terrain, that rapid destabilization can trigger wet-snow avalanches.

thermal stratification intensification.name: Thermal Stratification Intensification
thermal stratification intensification.description: Warming and freshening strengthen density layering in coastal and shelf waters, reducing vertical mixing, oxygen renewal, and resilience against low-oxygen events.
incoming: Upper-ocean warming strengthens density layering that limits mixing and can reduce vertical mixing, especially in coastal and shelf systems already sensitive to ventilation loss. Warming and freshening strengthen density layering in coastal and shelf waters, reducing vertical mixing, oxygen renewal, and resilience against low-oxygen events.
outgoing: A stronger density boundary limits vertical mixing and slows oxygen resupply to bottom water while respiration continues below the surface layer. Stronger thermal layering that limits mixing can increase shelf-sea hypoxia risk by suppressing exchange and oxygen ventilation below the mixed layer, especially where organic-carbon production and respiratory demand are already high.

Layered warm estuarine waters can worsen oxygen stress and habitat quality for juvenile fish and shellfish, narrowing nursery resilience. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of thermal layering that limits mixing intensification.

Stronger layering that limits mixing limits oxygen renewal from surface waters and is a well-established contributor to hypoxia risk in nutrient-loaded coastal waters. Thermal Stratification Intensification raises risk of by restricting oxygen renewal in coastal and shelf waters.

Seasonal thermal layering that limits mixing reduces vertical mixing and can limit nutrient delivery and primary production. At the Gulf of Lions study site, the stratified low-productivity season coincided with contraction of total benthic isotopic niche space, especially among low-trophic-level consumers, consistent with a narrower food-web resource base.

A more stable warm surface layer restricts mixed-layer depth, ventilation, and the transport of human-caused carbon away from the surface. Warming-driven upper-ocean layering that limits mixing reduces vertical exchange and contributes to lower ocean carbon-sink efficiency.

Stronger upper-ocean layering that limits mixing can isolate sunlit surface waters from deeper nutrient inventories, reducing nutrient supply and phytoplankton productivity in nutrient-limited regions. Added only after semantic node-class triage showed that a real causal-driver relationship, rather than a class exemption, was required.

incoming: Higher coastal water levels allow saline water to penetrate farther inland through estuaries, deltas, and connected coastal aquifers, especially during low-flow periods. Prolonged drought reduces river flow and estuarine flushing, allowing saline fronts to penetrate farther inland and persist longer. Extends when prolonged low-flow conditions allow saline fronts to move farther inland.
outgoing: Salt intrusion can threaten freshwater intakes and raise treatment difficulty, forcing utilities to manage salinity spikes, blending limits, and intake shifts. Threatens when saline water intrudes into source intakes and treatment systems.

Advancing saline fronts and tidal pressure can intensify intrusion into shallow coastal freshwater bodies, thinning already vulnerable freshwater lenses. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of delta salt intrusion fronts increases.

Salt-front migration is a practical process into coastal aquifer degradation because it increases salinization pressure in connected estuarine and delta groundwater systems. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of delta salt intrusion fronts.

extreme precipitation intensity.name: Extreme Precipitation Intensity
extreme precipitation intensity.description: A warmer atmosphere can dump more water in short bursts, increasing the intensity of rainfall events that overwhelm drainage, utilities, and river management systems.
incoming: Warmer air can contain more water vapour, increasing moisture convergence and event-scale precipitation intensity when lifting and storm dynamics are present. Additional warming increases the moisture ceiling available to the heaviest precipitation events.

nature-based adaptation.description: Wetlands, mangroves, urban trees, healthy soils, dunes, reefs, and connected habitats can reduce flood, heat, erosion, and water risks while supporting biodiversity.
incoming: Provides the ecological foundation for through healthy, connected, and maintained systems. Wetlands, mangroves, urban trees, healthy soils, dunes, reefs, and connected habitats can reduce flood, heat, erosion, and water risks while supporting biodiversity.
outgoing: Nature-Based Adaptation can finance and sustain Ecosystem Restoration when protective benefits are tied to long-term stewardship. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.
Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains

Nature-Based Adaptation reduces Floodplain Exposure through wetlands, floodplain reconnection, and upstream water retention. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Nature-Based Adaptation can reduce exposure to Coastal Inundation Risk through mangroves, marshes, dunes, and reefs within their physical limits. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Nature-Based Adaptation reduces Nighttime Heat Retention through shade, water loss from soil and plants, and less heat-absorbing surface. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Nature-Based Adaptation can reduce Biodiversity Intactness Loss when projects restore native, connected habitat. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

aquifer overdraft.name: Aquifer Overdraft
aquifer overdraft.description: Groundwater withdrawal that exceeds the rate at which an aquifer can recharge. Sustained pumping can draw saline groundwater upward or inland; repeated use of mineralized irrigation water then leaves salts in the root zone as water evaporates or is taken up by crops.
incoming: Irrigation water inefficiency intensifies aquifer overdraft when avoidable losses are replaced through pumping. Low irrigation application or conveyance efficiency can increase gross groundwater withdrawals and contribute to aquifer overdraft where pumping persistently exceeds recharge and return flows.

Water Reuse and Recycling reduces pressure on Aquifer Overdraft when reuse displaces groundwater withdrawals. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Climate-Resilient Agriculture can reduce Aquifer Overdraft when water efficiency is paired with basin withdrawal limits. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Sustained groundwater withdrawals that exceed natural or managed recharge turn wider resource pressure into measurable aquifer overdraft. Aquifer overdraft is a direct resource-depletion process where extraction continues past recharge for years or decades.
outgoing: Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands

Overpumping lowers freshwater heads and makes small-island lenses more vulnerable to saltwater intrusion and usable-storage loss. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of aquifer overdraft.
Pumping above recharge depletes groundwater storage and lowers water availability in monitored wells. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of aquifer overdraft.
Overpumping coastal aquifers lowers freshwater heads and increases depletion and saltwater-intrusion pressure. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of aquifer overdraft increases.
Sustained pumping can draw saline groundwater upward or inland. Repeated use of mineralized irrigation water then leaves salts in the root zone as water evaporates or is taken up by crops.

Overpumping coastal aquifers lowers freshwater heads and increases depletion and saltwater-intrusion pressure. Downstream changes in Coastal Aquifer Salinization can then affect water security and sanitation through Drinking Water Treatment Stress.

river flow regime change.name: River Flow Regime Change
river flow regime change.description: A persistent departure in river flow regime from its earlier pattern or state. When river discharge weakens or shifts seasonally, freshwater resistance to estuarine salinity intrusion drops and inland salt fronts can move farther upstream.
incoming: Higher global temperatures change river-flow timing and volume through evaporation, precipitation, snowmelt, and runoff timing. That can move peak flows earlier, deepen low-flow periods, and make water supplies less predictable.

Snowmelt timing shift advances river flow regime shift by moving runoff away from historical seasonal timing. Earlier snowmelt can shift snow-fed river flow toward earlier seasonal runoff and reduce warm-season contribution where storage and rainfall do not compensate.
Through reduced and earlier snowmelt runoff, Snow Drought intensifies River Flow Regime Change. Rivers then receive a smaller, earlier spring pulse and less water during the warm season.

Glacier outburst floods release stored meltwater abruptly, producing discharge peaks far above normal seasonal flow. Repeated drainage events can shift the timing, magnitude and sediment load of downstream river flow.

Storage, diversion, and operating rules can suppress seasonal peaks, change daily fluctuations, and alter the timing and volume of downstream discharge. Dams, diversions, poorly designed road-stream crossings, levees and channelization can impede aquatic passage, disconnect floodplains or stream reaches, and alter the timing, magnitude, velocity or local distribution of river flow.

Constriction, perched outlets, and crossing geometry can change local velocity, depth, sediment transport, and channel form relative to an unimpeded reference reach. Dams, diversions, poorly designed road-stream crossings, levees and channelization can impede aquatic passage, disconnect floodplains or stream reaches, and alter the timing, magnitude, velocity or local distribution of river flow.

Confinement and straightening can accelerate downstream transport, change water depth and velocity, alter inundation frequency, and separate the main channel from floodplain storage. Dams, diversions, poorly designed road-stream crossings, levees and channelization can impede aquatic passage, disconnect floodplains or stream reaches, and alter the timing, magnitude, velocity or local distribution of river flow.

Sustained heavy precipitation can raise runoff and streamflow sharply, especially when soils are saturated, snow melts, or terrain focuses rainfall into a river network. Many detected events replenish water supplies without damaging flow, while dry soils, storage, weak lift, or short duration can limit runoff.
outgoing: When river discharge weakens or shifts seasonally, freshwater resistance to estuarine salinity intrusion drops and inland salt fronts can move farther upstream. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of river flow regime change.

River flow regime shift destabilizes reservoir storage instability when inflow timing and volume depart from operating assumptions. Reservoirs may then refill at the wrong time or fail to hold enough water for dry-season demand.

River flow regime shift pressures basin treaty breakdown when historical allocation rules no longer match available flow. Allocation rules based on historical flows can become harder to honor, increasing conflict between upstream and downstream users.

River flow regime shift creates reservoir operating shortfall when release rules cannot match altered inflow timing. Operators may then miss flood-control, hydropower, water-supply, or environmental-flow targets.

Hydropower reliability falls when river timing and seasonal flow patterns no longer match reservoir and turbine expectations. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of river flow regime change.

human.summary: River Flow Regime Change can affect water security and sanitation and essential services and infrastructure through Reservoir Operating Shortfall, Hydropower Reliability Decline, and Drinking Water Treatment Stress.
consequences: River flow regime shift creates reservoir operating shortfall when release rules cannot match altered inflow timing.
Hydropower reliability falls when river timing and seasonal flow patterns no longer match reservoir and turbine expectations.

planet.summary: River Flow Regime Change directly changes biodiversity, habitat, and ecosystem resilience, measured through Daily mean stream discharge anomaly.
consequences: When river discharge weakens or shifts seasonally, freshwater resistance to estuarine salinity intrusion drops and inland salt fronts can move farther upstream.
River flow regime shift destabilizes reservoir storage instability when inflow timing and volume depart from operating assumptions.

response.defaultDriver: Temp changes river flow regime shift through evaporation, precipitation, snowmelt, and runoff timing.
levers: Address the verified upstream pressures that increase River Flow Regime Change rather than treating the observed outcome in isolation.
Use Daily mean stream discharge anomaly to test whether policy or operational changes are reducing the condition.

measurement.metric: Daily mean stream discharge anomaly
measurement.geography: USGS monitoring station and basin
measurement.cadence: daily snapshot

reservoir storage instability.name: Reservoir Storage Instability
reservoir storage instability.description: Greater variability and reduced reliability in reservoir storage. Reservoir-storage instability becomes operationally visible when managers can no longer count on expected usable storage, release timing, or generation support.
incoming: River flow regime shift destabilizes reservoir storage instability when inflow timing and volume depart from operating assumptions. Reservoirs may then refill at the wrong time or fail to hold enough water for dry-season demand.
Through prolonged inflow deficits, Drought Persistence deepens Reservoir Storage Instability. As inflows remain low, reservoirs may not refill enough to meet water, power, and ecological needs.

Through diminished seasonal snowpack storage, Snow Drought raises Reservoir Storage Instability. Reservoirs may refill earlier but still enter summer with less stored water for farms, cities, and ecosystems.

Suspended and bed material settles as flow velocity declines in impoundments, progressively occupying storage and affecting intakes where loads are sustained. How strongly this effect develops depends on reservoir geometry, flushing operations, and grain size.
outgoing: Reservoir-storage instability becomes operationally visible when managers can no longer count on expected usable storage, release timing, or generation support. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of reservoir storage instability.

human.summary: Reservoir Storage Instability can affect water security and sanitation through Reservoir Operating Shortfall.
consequences: Reservoir-storage instability becomes operationally visible when managers can no longer count on expected usable storage, release timing, or generation support.

planet.summary: Reservoir Storage Instability directly changes freshwater timing, quality, and aquatic habitat, measured through Reservoir storage instability.
consequences: Reservoir-storage instability becomes operationally visible when managers can no longer count on expected usable storage, release timing, or generation support.

response.defaultDriver: Upstream deforestation and soil erosion accelerate silt buildup, and old dams lack flushing gates.

reservoir operating shortfall.name: Reservoir Operating Shortfall
reservoir operating shortfall.description: Insufficient usable storage or release flexibility to meet a reservoir’s expected water-supply, flood-control, or power obligations. Reservoir-storage instability becomes operationally visible when managers can no longer count on expected usable storage, release timing, or generation support.
incoming: Reservoir-storage instability becomes operationally visible when managers can no longer count on expected usable storage, release timing, or generation support. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of reservoir storage instability.

River flow regime shift creates reservoir operating shortfall when release rules cannot match altered inflow timing. Operators may then miss flood-control, hydropower, water-supply, or environmental-flow targets.
outgoing: Operating shortfalls are a direct process into hydropower reliability decline because constrained storage and release flexibility reduce dependable generation. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of reservoir operating shortfall.

human.summary: Reservoir Operating Shortfall directly represents pressure on water security and sanitation, measured through Reservoir storage deficit below a declared operating rule curve.
consequences: Operating shortfalls are a direct pathway into hydropower reliability decline because constrained storage and release flexibility reduce dependable generation.

response.defaultDriver: Reservoir operations were often designed around historical inflow timing and storage assumptions that are no longer stable.
levers: Updating reservoir rule curves to reflect altered runoff timing and drought carryover risk.
Investing in sediment management and forecasting to preserve usable storage volume.

shift in snowmelt timing.name: Shift in Snowmelt Timing
shift in snowmelt timing.description: A shift in when seasonal snow begins melting and when its runoff reaches downstream rivers and reservoirs. Earlier or faster snowmelt increases liquid water within the mountain snowpack and weakens its internal structure.
incoming: Darkening snow with black carbon lowers reflectivity and can accelerate earlier melt, making this a local frozen-water system process. Advances by lowering snow surface reflectivity and accelerating melt.

Warmer air causes snow to melt earlier, shifting the spring runoff peak and changing when rivers receive water from the seasonal snowpack. Across 2,339 snow-affected, minimally impaired Northern Hemisphere catchments, a 1 degree Celsius increase in catchment annual mean air temperature was associated on average with a 4.7-day advance in the annual maximum snowmelt-flood peak date, with a 5.0-day cross-catchment standard deviation.

A smaller or warmer seasonal snowpack often melts earlier and produces a weaker spring pulse, shifting the timing of runoff. Snow drought can condition snowmelt timing shift through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.

Carbon-dioxide emissions warm snow-dominated basins, causing winter precipitation to fall more often as rain and advancing the seasonal timing of snowmelt. Cumulative greenhouse-gas emissions alter heat trapped in the climate system and climate, which can change snow accumulation and melt timing, drought and heavy-precipitation conditions, flood-generating processes, water quality and freshwater ecosystems.

Dark mineral particles reduce snow surface reflectivity, increase shortwave-energy absorption, accelerate grain growth and melt, and expose darker ground earlier, shifting melt and peak runoff toward earlier dates. Fresh snowfall can temporarily bury dust, cloud cover reduces shortwave forcing, and the magnitude cannot be transferred between basins without local snow-energy modeling.
outgoing: Earlier or faster snowmelt can shift runoff timing and intensify melt-season flow pulses, especially where storage is limited. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of shift in snowmelt timing increases.

Snowmelt timing shift advances river flow regime shift by moving runoff away from historical seasonal timing. Earlier snowmelt can shift snow-fed river flow toward earlier seasonal runoff and reduce warm-season contribution where storage and rainfall do not compensate.

Earlier or faster snowmelt increases liquid water within the mountain snowpack and weakens its internal structure. Wet-snow avalanche risk can rise when saturated layers lose cohesion above exposed passes.
Earlier snowmelt delivers water to glacier drainage systems sooner and can raise pressure before channels are fully developed. Rapid reorganization or blockage can release stored water as a flood.

Earlier snowmelt changes the seasonal timing and apparent composition of mountain runoff, helping expose when former glacier-melt buffering no longer sustains late-season flow. Some glacier-fed basins are moving past the stage of rising meltwater supply and into long-term decline, changing the reliability of downstream seasonal water systems.

Earlier loss of seasonal snow can reduce the duration and extent of cool, moist snowbed microhabitat on alpine or polar nunataks, exposing specialised biota to longer growing-season heat and desiccation. Named nunatak or alpine snowbed with snow disappearance date, soil moisture and temperature, mapped microhabitat and species occupancy measured together.

human.summary: Shift in Snowmelt Timing can affect essential services and infrastructure and water security and sanitation through Bridge Scour Exposure, Reservoir Operating Shortfall, and Critical Infrastructure Fragility.
consequences: Earlier or faster snowmelt can shift runoff timing and intensify melt-season flow pulses, especially where storage is limited. Downstream changes in Rapid Runoff Response can then affect essential services and infrastructure through Bridge Scour Exposure.

Snowmelt timing shift advances river flow regime shift by moving runoff away from historical seasonal timing. Downstream changes in River Flow Regime Change can then affect water security and sanitation through Reservoir Operating Shortfall.

consequences: Earlier or faster snowmelt can shift runoff timing and intensify melt-season flow pulses, especially where storage is limited.
Snowmelt timing shift advances river flow regime shift by moving runoff away from historical seasonal timing.

levers: Cut the greenhouse-gas emissions that intensify Shift in Snowmelt Timing while distinguishing global forcing from local attribution.
Monitor Center of timing of snowmelt-derived runoff consistently so adaptation decisions follow the observed rate, location, and season of change.

measurement.metric: Center of timing of snowmelt-derived runoff
measurement.geography: named glacier, ice sheet sector, snow basin, permafrost region, or polar analysis grid

soil moisture collapse.name: Soil Moisture Collapse
soil moisture collapse.description: Active tracking of satellite-derived soil moisture anomalies; requires CDS/Earthdata logins for programmatic data access.
incoming: Persistent precipitation deficit and evaporative demand can drive soil moisture to exceptionally low levels when storage is not replenished. Research supports this direct process: drought_persistence drives soil_moisture_collapse when root-zone moisture cannot recover seasonally.
Higher temperatures draw more water from soil and plants. When rain cannot replace that loss, large areas can enter severe soil-moisture drought.

High atmospheric evaporative demand pulls water from soils and plants faster, accelerating root-zone drying when rainfall cannot replace the loss. Atmospheric dryness can condition soil moisture collapse through the reviewed water mechanism.

Carbon-dioxide-driven warming increases evaporation and plant water demand, drawing moisture from the root zone faster. Soil moisture can fall sharply when rainfall and irrigation do not replace those losses.
outgoing: Through persistent root-zone water stress, Soil Moisture Collapse increases Crop Yield Volatility. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of soil moisture collapse.
Soil moisture collapse raises pressure on groundwater depletion wells when irrigation shifts toward pumping. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of soil moisture collapse.

Severely dry soil suppresses evaporative cooling and shifts surface energy into heat, reinforcing atmospheric dryness above the land. Soil moisture collapse can condition atmospheric dryness through the reviewed extremes mechanism.

human.summary: Soil Moisture Collapse can affect food security and livelihoods through Crop Yield Volatility.
consequences: Through persistent root-zone water stress, Soil Moisture Collapse increases Crop Yield Volatility.

Severely dry soil suppresses evaporative cooling and shifts surface energy into heat, reinforcing atmospheric dryness above the land. Downstream changes in Atmospheric Evaporative Demand can then affect food security and livelihoods through Crop Yield Volatility.

planet.summary: Active tracking of satellite-derived soil moisture anomalies; requires CDS/Earthdata logins for programmatic data access.
consequences: Soil moisture collapse raises pressure on groundwater depletion wells when irrigation shifts toward pumping.
Severely dry soil suppresses evaporative cooling and shifts surface energy into heat, reinforcing atmospheric dryness above the land.

levers: Transitioning to conservation agriculture practices that maintain continuous organic soil cover.
Expanding root-zone soil moisture monitoring arrays to manage early water conservation.

flash flood regime.name: Flash Flood Regime
flash flood regime.description: The recurring pattern, timing, and severity of fast-rising floods after intense rain or sudden water release. Standing water, damaged drainage, altered water storage, and service disruption can increase mosquito breeding and human-vector contact.
incoming: Heavier short-duration rainfall increases flash-flood risk when rainfall rates overwhelm local drainage, infiltration, and channel capacity. More intense short-duration precipitation can increase the frequency or magnitude of pluvial and flash flooding when rainfall rates exceed local infiltration, channel, storage or artificial-drainage capacity.

Greater atmospheric moisture can intensify short-duration rainfall, but flash flooding also depends on storm dynamics, terrain, drainage, and antecedent conditions. Greater atmospheric moisture can raise short-duration extreme-rainfall potential and thereby increase flash-flood hazard when storms, terrain, soils, drainage and antecedent wetness convert rainfall into rapid runoff.

Active Madden-Julian Oscillation convection can raise heavy-rainfall and flash-flood potential, conditional on regional moisture and terrain. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of madden-julian oscillation.

A warmer atmosphere can intensify short-duration rainfall extremes, making temperature an upstream driver of flash-flood regime change. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of warming increases.

Carbon Emission intensifies heavy rainfall and can increase flash-flood risk where terrain, soil, and drainage conditions permit. Cumulative greenhouse-gas emissions alter heat trapped in the climate system and climate, which can change snow accumulation and melt timing, drought and heavy-precipitation conditions, flood-generating processes, water quality and freshwater ecosystems.
outgoing: Short-duration flood pulses can exceed sewer and treatment capacity, making flash-flood regime change an upstream driver of overflow risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of flash flood regime.

Through turbidity, contamination, and intake disruption, Flash Flood Regime overloads Drinking Water Treatment Stress. Treatment plants may need to slow intake or add filtration and disinfection while contamination remains elevated.

Standing water, damaged drainage, altered water storage, and service disruption can increase mosquito breeding and human-vector contact. Flooding and associated water and sanitation disruption can create breeding habitat and increase exposure for some vector-borne diseases.

Floodwater can contaminate drinking-water facilities and increase exposure to water-borne pathogens where treatment and hygiene controls fail. Magnitude and timing require a named regional observation.

human.summary: Flash Flood Regime can affect water security and sanitation and health and safety through Drinking Water Treatment Stress, Vector-Borne Disease Expansion, and Waterborne Pathogen Outbreaks.
consequences: Through turbidity, contamination, and intake disruption, Flash Flood Regime overloads Drinking Water Treatment Stress.
Standing water, damaged drainage, altered water storage, and service disruption can increase mosquito breeding and human-vector contact.

consequences: Short-duration flood pulses can exceed sewer and treatment capacity, making flash-flood regime change an upstream driver of overflow risk.
Through turbidity, contamination, and intake disruption, Flash Flood Regime overloads Drinking Water Treatment Stress.

drought persistence.name: Drought Persistence
drought persistence.description: Monitors multi-season drought persistence and carryover effects in soil and reservoirs.
incoming: Persistent blocking suppresses storm passage and precipitation beneath the block, sustaining regional drought conditions. Persistent blocking can prolong regional drought by repeatedly diverting storm tracks and suppressing precipitation over the blocked region.

Persistent North Atlantic Oscillation phases can sustain regional precipitation deficits, but drought outcomes depend on season and location. Modulates through regional precipitation and storm-track anomalies.
The Pacific-North American pattern can steer rain away from a region for a season, helping drought persist. The result depends on the pattern phase and time of year.

Slow planetary-wave patterns can sustain rainfall suppression and drought, but attribution varies by event. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of persistent rossby wave patterns.
Warmer air pulls more water from soil and plants. Where rain does not replace that loss, drought can become more severe and last longer.

Arctic Oscillation phases alter pressure, storm-track and temperature patterns. In some regions and seasons, the resulting precipitation deficits, early warming, snowmelt and water loss from soil and plants can contribute to persistent dryness into the following season.

El Niño reorganizes tropical convection and atmospheric circulation, producing sustained rainfall deficits in some regions. Weather deficits can persist through soil-moisture, river-flow, reservoir and peatland memory after the atmospheric anomaly develops, extending agricultural, water-related and fire-weather drought conditions.

Carbon-dioxide emissions warm land and increase atmospheric demand for moisture. Where precipitation remains deficient, faster drying can deepen soil and vegetation stress and allow drought conditions to persist.
Compound climate hazards can include persistent agricultural and ecological drought in drying regions. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
outgoing: Prolonged drought reduces river flow and estuarine flushing, allowing saline fronts to penetrate farther inland and persist longer. Extends when prolonged low-flow conditions allow saline fronts to move farther inland.
Through prolonged inflow deficits, Drought Persistence deepens Reservoir Storage Instability. As inflows remain low, reservoirs may not refill enough to meet water, power, and ecological needs.

Persistent precipitation deficit and evaporative demand can drive soil moisture to exceptionally low levels when storage is not replenished. Research supports this direct process: drought_persistence drives soil_moisture_collapse when root-zone moisture cannot recover seasonally.

Drought persistence raises pressure on basin treaty breakdown through repeated cross-border allocation shortfalls. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of drought persistence increases.

Drought persistence intensifies drinking water treatment stress through lower source volume and concentrated contaminants. Utilities may need more intensive treatment as pollutants and salts become concentrated in smaller water volumes.
Drought persistence increases risk of hydropower reliability decline through sustained inflow and head deficits. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of drought persistence.

Drought persistence raises risk of peat oxidation pulse through peat drying and oxygen exposure. Peat oxidation is treated as a carbon-cycle feedback because the United States space agency Earthdata maintains peatland data access and monitoring processes relevant to peat carbon storage, drainage, fire, and release risk.

Persistent drought dries soils and reduces evaporative cooling, leaving crops, livestock and farm workers exposed to hotter local conditions. Drought persistence can condition farm heat stress through the reviewed food mechanism.

Persistent drought dries live and dead vegetation across seasons, increasing the amount of burnable fuel and lengthening the period of elevated fire risk. Drought persistence can condition wildfire regime shift through the reviewed extremes mechanism.

Persistent drought reduces aquifer recharge while often increasing pumping demand, accelerating groundwater depletion where withdrawals already approach sustainable limits. Aquifers are being drawn down faster than they recharge, turning hidden water reserves into a long-lived constraint on farming, drinking water, and ecosystem resilience.

Persistent drought reduces surface supply and groundwater recharge, increasing water stress when demand remains high. Persistent imbalance between water demand and available supply raises the baseline fragility of cities, farms, power systems, and river ecosystems.

Persistent drought reduces soil moisture and water loss from soil and plants, increasing sensible heating and atmospheric demand for water. Drought persistence can condition atmospheric dryness through the reviewed extremes mechanism.

consequences: Drought persistence intensifies drinking water treatment stress through lower source volume and concentrated contaminants.
Drought persistence increases risk of hydropower reliability decline through sustained inflow and head deficits.

consequences: Prolonged drought reduces river flow and estuarine flushing, allowing saline fronts to penetrate farther inland and persist longer.

freshwater lens thinning in small island.name: Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands
freshwater lens thinning in small island.description: The thinning of the floating freshwater reserve beneath a small island as pumping, drought, or saltwater intrusion reduces its usable depth. When thin freshwater lenses can no longer supply reliable potable water, communities often become more dependent on desalination or imported water.
incoming: Rising sea level can thin and salinize shallow freshwater lenses on small islands by increasing saltwater intrusion pressure from below and the coast. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of sea-level rise increases.

Overpumping lowers freshwater heads and makes small-island lenses more vulnerable to saltwater intrusion and usable-storage loss. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of aquifer overdraft.

Advancing saline fronts and tidal pressure can intensify intrusion into shallow coastal freshwater bodies, thinning already vulnerable freshwater lenses. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of delta salt intrusion fronts increases.
Carbon Emission contributes to sea-level rise and coastal flooding pressures that can compress freshwater lenses on low islands. Downstream attribution is indirect unless stated otherwise.
outgoing: Through salinity and reduced potable-water availability, Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands increases Drinking Water Treatment Stress. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of freshwater lens thinning in small islands.

When thin freshwater lenses can no longer supply reliable potable water, communities often become more dependent on desalination or imported water. Pushes toward when thin coastal freshwater reserves can no longer meet reliable demand.

human.summary: Thin coastal freshwater reserves become a human crisis when shallow groundwater turns brackish, forcing households and utilities toward more expensive and fragile water supply options.
consequences: Water that still exists physically can become too saline or unreliable to use without expensive treatment.
Utilities and households spend more on storage, imported water, or desalination when shallow lenses fail.

drinking water treatment stress.name: Drinking Water Treatment Stress
drinking water treatment stress.description: Pressure on drinking water treatment severe enough to impair normal function or recovery. Persistent treatment stress from salinity and source-water degradation can harden into a shift toward desalination where utilities need a more salt-tolerant supply option.
incoming: Bypass discharge can raise contaminant and turbidity loads in receiving waters, increasing treatment difficulty and cost for downstream utilities. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of wastewater bypass discharge.

Forest loss in source watersheds can raise erosion, turbidity, and runoff volatility, increasing treatment strain for downstream drinking-water systems. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of watershed forest loss increases.

Salt intrusion can threaten freshwater intakes and raise treatment difficulty, forcing utilities to manage salinity spikes, blending limits, and intake shifts. Threatens when saline water intrudes into source intakes and treatment systems.
Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands

Through salinity and reduced potable-water availability, Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands increases Drinking Water Treatment Stress. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of freshwater lens thinning in small islands.

As coastal groundwater becomes more saline or degraded, utilities and users lose raw-water flexibility and face higher treatment and substitution burdens. Coastal Aquifer Salinization raises when salinized groundwater reduces raw-water quality and supply flexibility.

Coastal flooding and saline inundation can degrade raw-water quality, impair intake operations, and raise treatment stress for exposed drinking-water systems. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of coastal inundation risk.

Through turbidity, contamination, and intake disruption, Flash Flood Regime overloads Drinking Water Treatment Stress. Treatment plants may need to slow intake or add filtration and disinfection while contamination remains elevated.

Drought persistence intensifies drinking water treatment stress through lower source volume and concentrated contaminants. Utilities may need more intensive treatment as pollutants and salts become concentrated in smaller water volumes.
outgoing: Persistent treatment stress from salinity and source-water degradation can harden into a shift toward desalination where utilities need a more salt-tolerant supply option. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of drinking water treatment stress.

watershed forest loss.name: Watershed Forest Loss
watershed forest loss.description: The removal or death of forest cover within a drainage basin. Loss of watershed and bank vegetation can increase runoff and sediment delivery while reducing root reinforcement at exposed banks.
incoming: Warming and drying pressure raise watershed forest stress by increasing fire exposure, water loss from soil and plants pressure, and hydrologic instability across forested basins. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of warming increases.

Clearing forest within a watershed removes canopy and root structure, reducing forest cover while increasing erosion and rapid runoff into streams. Deforestation can condition watershed forest loss through the reviewed biodiversity mechanism.

Repeated severe fires can convert forested watersheds to lower-cover vegetation when tree mortality outpaces regeneration. Wildfire regime shift can condition watershed forest loss through the reviewed biodiversity mechanism.
outgoing: Loss of forest cover in key watersheds can degrade stream habitat, sediment conditions, and ecological buffering, pushing freshwater ecosystems toward collapse. Degrades toward through erosion and runoff change.

Forest loss in source watersheds can raise erosion, turbidity, and runoff volatility, increasing treatment strain for downstream drinking-water systems. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of watershed forest loss increases.

Watershed forest degradation can destabilize runoff timing and sediment conditions that matter for dependable hydropower operations. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of watershed forest loss.

Watershed forest loss intensifies riverine habitat fragmentation through erosion, channel alteration, and riparian loss. Sediment, warmer water, and damaged streambanks can isolate habitat and disrupt fish movement.

Loss of safe water and sanitation controls can expose people to pathogen-contaminated water and raise outbreak risk after flooding or system failure.
incoming: Short-duration flood pulses can exceed sewer and treatment capacity, making flash-flood regime change an upstream driver of overflow risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of flash flood regime.

Higher baseline coastal water levels can impair drainage and push wastewater systems toward backup and overflow during storms or high tides. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of coastal inundation risk.

More intense short-duration precipitation can exceed sewer conveyance and treatment-system design capacity, increasing overflow risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of extreme precipitation intensity.

Flood-Resilient Infrastructure reduces Wastewater Infrastructure Overflow through separated flows, added capacity, storage, and floodproofing. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.
outgoing: Overflow conditions often manifest operationally as bypass or emergency discharge events when plants and sewers exceed safe handling limits. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of wastewater infrastructure overflow.

When a combined wastewater system is hydraulically overloaded, discharge from its designated outfall is a combined sewer overflow. Applies only where a combined sewer system and a documented overflow process exist.

wastewater bypass discharge.description: Untreated or partly treated wastewater released around a normal treatment step during overload, failure, or maintenance. Untreated or bypassed wastewater delivers nitrogen and phosphorus to receiving waters.
incoming: Overflow conditions often manifest operationally as bypass or emergency discharge events when plants and sewers exceed safe handling limits. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of wastewater infrastructure overflow.

irrigation water inefficiency.name: Irrigation Water Inefficiency
irrigation water inefficiency.description: The loss of irrigation water before it benefits crops through evaporation, leakage, runoff, or poorly matched application. Inefficient irrigation requires more pumping for each unit of crop production, depleting aquifers when the additional withdrawal is not returned as usable recharge.
incoming: Industry farming can embed irrigation water inefficiency through poorly matched application and conveyance losses. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of industry farming.
outgoing: Irrigation water inefficiency intensifies aquifer overdraft when avoidable losses are replaced through pumping. Low irrigation application or conveyance efficiency can increase gross groundwater withdrawals and contribute to aquifer overdraft where pumping persistently exceeds recharge and return flows.

Irrigation water inefficiency deepens groundwater depletion wells through higher withdrawals per unit of crop output. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of irrigation water inefficiency.

ice sheet mass loss.description: Compiles satellite observations of Greenland and Antarctic ice sheet mass loss.
incoming: Higher air temperatures increase surface melting, while ocean warming can erode floating ice shelves and speed the discharge of grounded ice into the ocean. Compiles satellite observations of Greenland and Antarctic ice sheet mass loss.
Through cumulative greenhouse warming, Carbon Emission drives pressure toward Ice Sheet Mass Loss. Compiles satellite observations of Greenland and Antarctic ice sheet mass loss.

Warm subsurface ocean water increases basal melting beneath floating ice shelves, weakening their support for grounded ice and accelerating ice-sheet loss. Compiles satellite observations of Greenland and Antarctic ice sheet mass loss.
Loss of Firn Meltwater Storage Capacity

Loss of firn pore space and formation of impermeable ice layers reduce refreezing and retention capacity, allowing a larger share of surface meltwater to run off and contribute to ice-sheet mass loss. Compiles satellite observations of Greenland and Antarctic ice sheet mass loss.
outgoing: Antarctic meltwater freshens shelf waters and can inhibit formation of dense bottom water. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of ice sheet mass loss.

Observed sectoral ice mass loss and acceleration can signal reduced buttressing and a dynamic response associated with ice-shelf thinning or retreat, requiring mechanism-specific interpretation. Named Antarctic drainage basin and adjoining shelf only.
Ice loss can alter meltwater routing and flood hazards where impoundments, drainage processes, and exposure are present. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Fresh meltwater from Greenland lowers North Atlantic surface salinity and density, making deep-water formation less efficient and potentially weakening Atlantic overturning. Weakening Atlantic overturning circulation can redistribute heat, alter European and tropical rainfall, and increase the risk of abrupt regional climate disruptions.

Fresh meltwater from ice sheets lightens the ocean surface, strengthening the density barrier between surface and deeper water. Ice sheet mass loss can condition ocean salinity layering that limits mixing through the reviewed oceans mechanism.

Retreat and thinning can expose stored subglacial material and reorganize drainage, changing the amount and timing of sediment delivered to a glacier-fed basin. How strongly this effect develops depends on subglacial storage, bed geology, and retreat geometry.

Loss of land ice transfers water to the ocean and contributes directly to global mean sea-level rise. Observed Greenland Ice Sheet mass loss during 1992-2020 is equivalent to a 13.5 mm contribution to global mean sea level, with an assessed 11.4-15.6 mm range.
Ice-sheet-driven sea-level rise increases coastal inundation risk where exposure, tides, storms, and local land motion align. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
Higher sea level can allow waves and storm surge to act farther inland, increasing erosion risk on susceptible coasts. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
Sea-level rise can increase saline-water pressure in coastal aquifers, moderated by pumping, geology, recharge, and drainage. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
Sea-level rise raises the baseline for compound coastal flooding when surge, rainfall, river flow, or tides coincide. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
Loss of reflective land ice exposes darker surfaces and can reinforce local warming feedbacks, subject to surface conditions. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

glacial lake outburst flood risk.name: Glacial Lake Outburst Flood Risk
glacial lake outburst flood risk.description: The likelihood or potential severity of glacial lake outburst flood. Failure of an ice- or moraine-dammed glacial lake releases stored water into the glacier-fed drainage network.
incoming: At an ice-contact moraine-dammed lake, rapid frontal retreat and calving can remove support from an ice-rich lateral moraine or add iceberg volume to a landslide-generated displacement wave. The resulting slope failure, wave run-up, overtopping, or outlet erosion can contribute to dam breach.

Warming retreats glaciers and can enlarge unstable meltwater lakes, increasing outburst-flood risk where moraine or ice dams are weak. Higher global temperatures can condition glacial lake failure risk through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.
Carbon Emission drives glacier retreat and meltwater-lake change, increasing hazard where unstable lakes and exposed communities coexist. Downstream attribution is indirect unless stated otherwise.
outgoing: When a glacial lake dam fails, stored meltwater can drain suddenly and send a powerful surge into downstream rivers. The sudden pulse can overwhelm river channels and threaten communities, roads, and bridges downstream.

Through abrupt high-energy flood flows, Glacial Lake Outburst Flood Risk raises Bridge Scour Exposure. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of glacial lake outburst flood risk.

Failure of an ice- or moraine-dammed glacial lake releases stored water into the glacier-fed drainage network. The resulting outburst creates an abrupt downstream flood with high discharge and sediment load.

sea ice season loss.name: Sea Ice Season Loss
sea ice season loss.description: A shortening of the part of the year when a region remains covered by sea ice. A longer ice-free season can extend Arctic navigation windows, although mobile ice, severe weather, port access, insurance and regulation still determine whether shipping expands.
incoming: Higher global temperatures melt Arctic sea ice earlier and delay its return in autumn, shortening the annual sea-ice season. At stabilized global warming of 2 degrees Celsius, the assessed annual probability of a practically sea-ice-free Arctic September by the end of the century is 10-35 percent, compared with approximately 1 percent at 1.5 degrees Celsius.

Ocean heat melts sea ice from below and delays autumn freeze-up, shortening the period of seasonal ice cover. Ocean heat content can condition sea ice season loss through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.

Rapid Arctic warming accelerates spring melt and delays autumn freeze-up, shortening the annual sea-ice season. Arctic amplification rates can condition sea ice season loss through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.
Carbon dioxide emissions warm the Arctic, causing sea ice to melt earlier and form later. This shortens the season when the ocean remains ice-covered.

coastal inundation risk.description: The likelihood or potential severity of coastal inundation. Storm surge, astronomical tide and sea-level rise combine to inundate low-elevation coastal assets.

outgoing: Higher baseline coastal water levels can impair drainage and push wastewater systems toward backup and overflow during storms or high tides. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of coastal inundation risk.

Salt fronts can push farther inland in deltas and estuaries as sea level rises, river discharge weakens, and storm-driven water levels press saline water into farms and intakes.

Repeated coastal flooding and higher saline water tables can degrade connected coastal groundwater, especially where aquifers are shallow and hydraulically exposed. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of coastal inundation risk.

snow drought.name: Snow Drought
snow drought.description: An unusually small snowpack, or an early loss of stored snow, that reduces dependable cold-season water storage. A smaller or warmer seasonal snowpack often melts earlier and produces a weaker spring pulse, shifting the timing of runoff.
incoming: Warming shifts precipitation phase and accelerates snow loss, making higher temperature an upstream driver of snow-drought risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of warming.

Carbon-dioxide-driven warming causes more winter precipitation to fall as rain and accelerates melt from the snowpack. Mountain basins can enter snow drought when seasonal snow-water storage falls well below its expected level.
outgoing: Through reduced and earlier snowmelt runoff, Snow Drought intensifies River Flow Regime Change. Rivers then receive a smaller, earlier spring pulse and less water during the warm season.

Through diminished seasonal snowpack storage, Snow Drought raises Reservoir Storage Instability. Reservoirs may refill earlier but still enter summer with less stored water for farms, cities, and ecosystems.

Reduced snow accumulation decreases seasonal storage and can make basins more dependent on a shrinking glacier contribution, increasing post-peak late-season supply risk. Some glacier-fed basins are moving past the stage of rising meltwater supply and into long-term decline, changing the reliability of downstream seasonal water systems.

A snow drought leaves mountain snowpacks smaller because less snow falls, more rain falls instead, or warm weather melts the snow early. A snow-drought season reduces seasonal snow water storage through low snowfall, rain-on-snow conditions, or warm-season melt anomalies.

Persistent snow-accumulation deficits reduce mass input to small ice caps. Where ablation remains high, negative surface mass balance can thin summit and connecting ice until formerly continuous cap geometry fragments.

outgoing: The phase of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation can make ocean heatwaves in the northeast Pacific more or less frequent, long-lasting, and intense. Observed Pacific Decadal Oscillation phase modulates Northeast Pacific marine-heatwave frequency, duration, and intensity.

marine fisheries collapse.name: Marine Fisheries Collapse
marine fisheries collapse.description: A severe loss of fish abundance or reproductive capacity that prevents a fishery from sustaining normal harvest and ecosystem roles. A sustained decline in accessible stock can reduce expected catch and revenue, intensifying competition among fleets or states where access is contested and institutions cannot adjust allocation peacefully.
incoming: When estuary nursery habitat declines, fewer young fish and shellfish survive to replenish coastal fisheries. Stocks can then become more vulnerable to collapse.

Deoxygenation contributes to fishery risk through habitat compression, mortality, and stock redistribution. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of oceanic deoxygenation.

Carbon emissions warm and alter the ocean, shifting habitats and reducing the productivity of some fish populations. Fisheries can decline when species cannot adapt or move fast enough.

Selective depletion of harvested predators or consumers can propagate through prey and lower trophic levels, but a trophic cascade requires measured intermediate and downstream responses rather than one declining taxon alone.

Changes in Southern Annular Mode winds can alter currents around Antarctica. The response depends on the pattern phase, location, and length of time involved.

incoming: Excess fertilizer nitrogen carried into coastal waters stimulates nutrient pollution and oxygen drawdown, contributing directly to coastal hypoxia. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of nitrogen fertilizer runoff.

Stronger layering that limits mixing limits oxygen renewal from surface waters and is a well-established contributor to hypoxia risk in nutrient-loaded coastal waters. Thermal Stratification Intensification raises risk of by restricting oxygen renewal in coastal and shelf waters.

Organic and nutrient loads from untreated or partially treated wastewater can increase oxygen demand and contribute to estuarine and nearshore hypoxia. Wastewater Bypass Discharge contributes to through oxygen-demanding organic and nutrient loads in estuaries and nearshore waters.

Dense bloom growth and decay can intensify oxygen drawdown, making harmful algal blooms a local contributor to coastal hypoxia. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of harmful algal blooms increases.

Warmer seawater holds less dissolved oxygen, can increase organism and microbial oxygen demand, and can strengthen or prolong density layering that limits mixing that limits ventilation of bottom waters. These processes can increase oxygen stress in susceptible coastal waters, while nutrient loading, circulation and runoff remain independent and often dominant controls.

Carbon-dioxide-driven warming reduces the amount of oxygen water can hold and can strengthen coastal layering that limits mixing. In nutrient-rich waters, weaker mixing and faster biological respiration increase the risk of low-oxygen events.

Nutrient losses from intensive agriculture can contribute to coastal hypoxia where downstream transport, loading, and oxygen response are documented. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

marine food-web reorganization.name: Marine Food-Web Reorganization
marine food-web reorganization.description: A reorganization of marine feeding relationships that leaves fewer functional groups, pathways, or resilient species. Food-web reorganization becomes socially visible when altered species composition and timing make local fish landings less reliable.
incoming: Redistributed pelagic species can reorganize trophic relationships and access to prey, making food-web reorganization a downstream effect. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of pelagic species redistribution.

Salinity-driven layering that limits mixing can reshape vertical mixing and nutrient availability, which in turn changes marine productivity and food-web structure. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of ocean salinity layering that limits mixing increases.

Changes in phytoplankton productivity and composition reorganize the food-web base available to higher marine trophic levels. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of phytoplankton decline.

Low oxygen compresses viable habitat and excludes oxygen-sensitive organisms, reorganizing marine communities. Persistent low oxygen can exclude or kill oxygen-sensitive organisms and favour tolerant taxa, simplifying local marine food-web structure when exposure exceeds species thresholds.
More acidic ocean water stresses sensitive species and changes who eats whom. These disruptions can simplify the food web and reduce energy available to larger animals.
Circulation shifts alter heat and nutrient transport, creating a specific process to food-web reorganization. Reorganizes through altered heat, nutrient, and habitat transport.
Ocean heatwaves can kill or weaken species at different levels of the food web. This disrupts how energy moves through the ecosystem and can reduce larger animals more severely.

Seasonal thermal layering that limits mixing reduces vertical mixing and can limit nutrient delivery and primary production. At the Gulf of Lions study site, the stratified low-productivity season coincided with contraction of total benthic isotopic niche space, especially among low-trophic-level consumers, consistent with a narrower food-web resource base.

Changes in ice-algae biomass and pigmentation alter the timing and amount of food available at the base of polar marine food webs. A weaker or mistimed algal pulse can reduce energy transfer to zooplankton and the fish, seabirds and mammals that feed above them.

Reduced growth or survival of calcifying shellfish and plankton can alter prey availability and habitat functions, contributing to food-web reorganization where they are ecologically important. Food webs with material dependence on the affected calcifying taxa.

Carbon emissions alter ocean temperature, acidity, oxygen and circulation, shifting which species can survive and where prey remains available. Repeated losses of sensitive or specialized species can simplify marine food-web structure.

ocean salinity stratification.name: Ocean Salinity Stratification
ocean salinity stratification.description: The layering of ocean water by salt content in ways that restrict vertical mixing. Freshening-driven density layering inhibits mixed-layer deepening, ventilation, and transfer of absorbed carbon into the ocean interior.
incoming: Ocean warming and added freshwater from land-ice loss strengthen density differences between surface and deeper water, limiting vertical mixing and reinforcing salinity-driven layering that limits mixing. Warming alters glacier and sea-ice energy balance, ocean heat and freshwater structure, and carbon uptake.

Fresh meltwater from ice sheets lightens the ocean surface, strengthening the density barrier between surface and deeper water. Ice sheet mass loss can condition ocean salinity layering that limits mixing through the reviewed oceans mechanism.

Heavy rainfall and runoff can freshen the ocean surface locally, strengthening short-lived layering that limits mixing when winds and mixing remain weak. Extreme precipitation intensity can condition ocean salinity layering that limits mixing through the reviewed oceans mechanism.

Carbon Emission alters evaporation, precipitation, ice melt, and warming patterns that can increase layering that limits mixing in affected basins. Greenhouse-gas emissions drive warming and carbon-cycle changes that can alter ocean heat, salinity, layering that limits mixing, oxygen, circulation and acidity.
outgoing: Changing salinity structure alters density gradients and circulation behavior, making layering that limits mixing a neighboring driver of broader circulation-regime shifts. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of ocean salinity layering that limits mixing.

Salinity-driven layering that limits mixing can reshape vertical mixing and nutrient availability, which in turn changes marine productivity and food-web structure. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of ocean salinity layering that limits mixing increases.

Layering that limits mixing restricts vertical ventilation and oxygen renewal in subsurface waters. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of ocean salinity layering that limits mixing increases.

Freshening-driven density layering inhibits mixed-layer deepening, ventilation, and transfer of absorbed carbon into the ocean interior. Stronger density layering that limits mixing can limit surface-interior exchange and carbon transport.
